For this disposable repository, configure a local practice author after git init: git config user.name "Practice Learner" and git config user.email "learner@example.invalid". Omit --global so you do not alter other repositories. The address is a fictional example, not a delivery destination. Use git status after every operation; it tells you what is staged, modified or untracked. If a commit fails, read its error before repeating commands; failure does not by itself delete your file.
guide.example:
mkdir git-lab
cd git-lab
git init
printf 'first version\n' > note.txt
git status --short
git add note.txt
git diff --cached
git commit -m 'docs: Add practice note'
printf 'second version\n' > note.txt
git diff
# Requires a locally configured Git author identity.
guide.explanation: Before staging, note.txt is untracked. After git add, its exact contents are in the index. The commit captures first version. The later edit appears in git diff but not in that existing commit. If author identity is missing, follow Git's setup documentation; the failure does not mean the file disappeared.
guide.exercise: Perform the shown local history. Stage the second version, inspect the staged diff and commit it. Use git log --oneline and git show to find the two versions. Record each commit's purpose in a separate nonsecret lab log.
guide.solution: Two commits show first version followed by second version. A clean status after the second commit means no current unstaged/staged edits, not that the history lacks sensitive material.
guide.challenge: In the disposable repository, first run git status and finish or save any uncommitted practice edits. Create a branch with git switch -c left, replace the note’s single line with left, then add and commit note.txt. Create another branch from the previous commit with git switch -c right HEAD~1, replace that same line with right, then add and commit it. While on right, run git merge left. Inspect the conflict, choose a deliberate final sentence, remove the marker lines, stage note.txt and commit. Explain why Git could not choose the sentence for you. This exercise stays local.
guide.challenge_solution: Both branches changed the same original line in different ways, so a conflict is expected. The file contains marker lines separating left and right alternatives. After choosing a sentence, verify the file has no marker lines and contains the intended text, then run git add note.txt and git commit with a message explaining the resolution. git log --graph --oneline shows a merge with two parents. A successful merge command alone is not enough: reread the final note. HEAD~1 in the supplied sequence means the commit immediately before the left-branch edit; confirm this history before using it elsewhere.

L03.concept: Git records snapshots of tracked files in commits. The working tree contains current files; the staging area selects what the next commit will contain. A commit message explains the change, while the diff shows the exact content. Version history supports investigation because you can compare states and identify when behaviour changed.
L03.mechanism: A repository should help another person reproduce your work. Include setup instructions, dependency information, test commands, and evidence references. Ignore generated caches and local secrets before adding files. Deleting a secret in a later commit does not erase earlier copies from history; credentials that have been exposed need replacement through the issuing system.
L03.example: Create a repository for a tiny parser. Commit the working version, change one validation rule, and inspect the diff before staging that file. Make a second commit with a clear explanation. Use git log and git show to recover the reasoning and content of the first version without guessing from today's files.
L03.pitfall: A repository backup and a progress backup solve different problems. Your browser notebook is not automatically committed with your code.

check.question: What determines which current changes enter the next Git commit?
choices: All files currently open in the editor
The staging area
The names in the last commit message
check.explanation: Git commits the staged snapshot. Unstaged working-tree edits remain outside that commit.

guide.bridge: Builds on M01 arithmetic and P02 tracing. Read the notation here before the formal lecture; no proof-writing experience is assumed.
guide.teaching:
Start with a rule you can challenge: “If an account is an administrator, it may edit.” It promises editing to administrators, but it does not say that nobody else may edit. A writer account could also have editing permission. In logic, P implies Q fails only when P is true and Q is false: the condition held but the promised consequence did not. When P is false, the promise says nothing about that case. It does not describe cause and effect.

AND means both conditions hold; OR means at least one holds, including both; NOT reverses true and false. A truth table lists every combination. For P and Q there are four rows: neither, Q only, P only, both. Translate symbols back into words until the notation is familiar.

A set records distinct members, such as the allowed names {Ada, Bea}. A function maps each input in its domain to exactly one output in its codomain; these words mean the allowed inputs and the declared output set. A graph draws objects as dots, called vertices, and relationships as lines, called edges. With arrows it is directed, so direction matters. A state machine describes states and permitted changes, called transitions. A guard is a condition that must hold before a transition may occur.

An invariant is true in every reachable state of the stated model. Check the initial state, then every permitted kind of transition. For a balance starting at 0, “balance is never negative” holds initially. A deposit of a non-negative amount preserves it. A withdrawal preserves it when the amount is non-negative and no greater than the balance. These checks explain why every later balance stays non-negative. This is induction: establish the start, then show that each next step preserves the claim. It covers the permitted model, not an implementation you have not checked.

To read the relation excerpt, first form a Cartesian product: if \(A=\{u,v\}\) and \(B=\{r,s\}\), then \(A\times B=\{(u,r),(u,s),(v,r),(v,s)\}\). A relation is any subset of these ordered pairs. For a relation on one set, reflexive means every element relates to itself; symmetric means \(xRy\Rightarrow yRx\); transitive means \(xRy\land yRz\Rightarrow xRz\). Antisymmetric means \(xRy\land yRx\Rightarrow x=y\). It is not the opposite of symmetry: equality is both symmetric and antisymmetric. A directed edge can represent one related pair. Mathematical implication describes truth conditions, not necessarily a causal mechanism.
guide.example:
P Q | P AND Q | P implies Q
F F | F       | T
F T | F       | T
T F | F       | F
T T | T       | T

Door states: Locked, Unlocked
unlock: Locked -> Unlocked, requires valid_key
lock: Unlocked -> Locked
Invariant: unlock succeeds only if valid_key is true.
guide.explanation: In the truth table, the implication is false only in row T,F: the stated condition holds but the promised result does not. The door example’s guard is a rule about when an unlock action is allowed. It does not require a key to remain present for as long as a door stays unlocked. Keep that action rule separate from a claim about every persistent state. The balance argument in the teaching section is a complete state-invariant example: start at zero and inspect each permitted balance-changing action.
guide.exercise: Build the truth table for NOT(P AND Q) and compare it with (NOT P) OR (NOT Q). Then add a maintenance transition to the door that requires admin=true. State a corrected authorisation invariant covering both routes.
guide.solution: The two expressions match in all four rows: T,T,T,F for FF,FT,TF,TT. The revised condition is that unlock requires valid_key OR admin, with each transition enforcing its own guard.
guide.challenge: A stock counter starts at 0 and must remain between 0 and 3 inclusive. A receive action adds an integer amount only when 0 <= amount <= 3-stock. A take action subtracts an integer amount only when 0 <= amount <= stock. Without copying the balance proof, explain why both bounds remain true after every action. Then remove the receive upper-bound check and give a sequence that breaks the invariant.
guide.challenge_solution: Base: stock=0 is within [0,3]. Receive adds a non-negative amount, so stock cannot fall below zero; its upper guard ensures the new value is at most 3. Take subtracts a non-negative amount, so stock cannot rise above 3; amount<=stock ensures it stays at least zero. Those are all permitted actions, so the bounds are preserved. Without the receive upper bound, receiving 4 from stock=0 gives stock=4, a counterexample. The proof assumes integer inputs and these exact guards.

M02.concept: Logic gives precise meaning to claims. A proposition is true or false; a conjunction requires both parts, while an implication says that whenever its premise holds, its conclusion must hold. Sets collect elements, functions map inputs to outputs, and graphs represent relationships using vertices and edges. These tools make security policies less ambiguous.
M02.mechanism: A state machine describes possible states and the transitions between them. An invariant is a property that must hold in every reachable state. To prove one by induction, show it holds initially and that each permitted transition preserves it. Testing several states can find a counterexample but does not replace reasoning over all permitted transitions.
M02.example: Model a document as private or shared, with read and share operations. Define the invariant: only an owner may change sharing. List every transition and the required actor. Find a transition that would violate the invariant if its permission check were omitted. Express the corrected rule as a condition over the actor and document owner.
M02.pitfall: An implication does not assert its premise. 'If administrator, then may edit' does not mean everyone who may edit is an administrator.

check.question: What makes a property an invariant of a state machine?
choices: It held during one successful demo
It holds initially and is preserved by every permitted transition
Its name contains the word secure
check.explanation: Initial truth plus preservation establishes the property across all reachable states covered by the model.

guide.bridge: From M01, divide 19 by 7: two groups use 14 and leave 5. From M02, distinguish the ordered pair AB from the unordered set {A,B}. You will work with small integers and list possibilities before using compact counting formulas.
guide.teaching:
A remainder is what is left after removing whole groups. For 19 divided by 7, remove 14 and keep 5; write 19 mod 7 = 5. On a 12-hour clock, moving five hours past 10 reaches 3 because 15 and 3 differ by a full turn of 12. Congruent means “same remainder for this modulus”; the symbol ≡ records that relationship.

A divisor divides a number without a remainder. The common positive divisors of 6 and 9 include 1 and 3; the greatest is 3, their greatest common divisor or gcd. Numbers with gcd 1 are coprime. An inverse is a multiplier that brings a product back to the remainder 1, the value that leaves multiplication unchanged. To find the inverse of 2 mod 5, try 1,2,3,4: their products leave 2,4,1,3. The successful multiplier is 3.

Modular arithmetic identifies integers with the same remainder after division by a positive modulus. Writing a≡b mod n means n divides a-b. With a 12-hour clock, 14 and 2 represent the same remainder. Addition and multiplication respect this equivalence, so intermediate results may be reduced without changing the final remainder.

Division needs care. A modular inverse of a is a value x such that ax≡1 mod n. It exists exactly when a and n have greatest common divisor 1. Ordinary division and modular inversion are not interchangeable. The Euclidean algorithm repeatedly takes remainders to compute the greatest common divisor; its steps can be reversed to find an inverse.

Counting depends on whether order and repetition matter. Three independent slots with two choices each give 2×2×2=8 sequences. Choosing two people from three without order gives three pairs, not six. Before applying a formula, state the outcome space. Later cryptographic arguments rely on these assumptions; a large-looking number is meaningless if the choices are predictable or correlated.

The quotient–remainder rule uses a positive divisor \(a\): \(b=qa+r\), with \(0\le r<a\). Bézout’s identity says that for integers \(a,b\), not both zero, integers \(s,t\) exist with \(sa+tb=\gcd(a,b)\). The worked inverse example below is back-substitution in this identity. A prime is an integer greater than one with exactly two positive divisors; one is not prime. For counting, \(n!=n(n-1)\cdots1\), with \(0!=1\), counts arrangements of distinct objects. Choosing \(k\) distinct objects without order gives \(\binom nk=n!/[k!(n-k)!]\): divide ordered selections by the \(k!\) orders of each chosen group. Repeated entries in set notation do not create new elements; a multiset is a different structure that records multiplicity.

In the worked calculation, -2 and 5 are equivalent modulo 7 because adding one full modulus gives -2+7=5. Negative intermediate coefficients are allowed; we choose the representative between 0 and 6 for the final answer. For the pairs exercise, write AB, AC, AD first, then BC, BD, then CD. BA is not a new unordered pair, and AA is excluded by “without repetition”. This list explains the six outcomes before the binomial formula abbreviates the counting.
guide.example:
Find inverse of 3 mod 7:
7 = 2*3 + 1
1 = 7 - 2*3
So (-2)*3 ≡ 1 mod 7; -2 ≡ 5 mod 7.
Check: 3*5 = 15 ≡ 1 mod 7.

But 2 has no inverse mod 6:
2*x mod 6 is always 0, 2 or 4, never 1.
guide.explanation: An inverse lets you undo multiplication only within the stated modulus. In the second case, common factor 2 prevents reaching remainder 1. For counting, list all two-bit sequences 00,01,10,11: order is visible because 01 and 10 differ.
guide.exercise: Calculate (8+11) mod 7 and (8*11) mod 7. Find the inverse of 2 mod 5 by enumeration. List all unordered pairs from {A,B,C,D} without repetition.
guide.solution: Remainders are 5 and 4. The inverse is 3 because 2*3=6≡1 mod 5. Pairs are AB,AC,AD,BC,BD,CD: six outcomes.
guide.challenge: Does 4 have an inverse mod 9? Show a check. Count length-three binary strings and unordered two-element subsets of a three-element set. Explain the difference in assumptions.
guide.challenge_solution: Inverse is 7 since 4*7=28≡1 mod 9. Binary strings: 8 ordered sequences with repetition. Two-element subsets: 3 unordered selections without repetition. These counts answer different questions.

M03.concept: Modular arithmetic wraps integers around a fixed modulus. On a twelve-hour clock, 10 + 5 is congruent to 3 modulo 12. A prime has exactly two positive divisors. Integers a and n are coprime when their greatest common divisor is 1. This relationship determines when a has a multiplicative inverse modulo n.
M03.mechanism: Counting describes how many possibilities exist before assigning probabilities. Independent choices multiply: four positions with ten choices each give 10,000 strings when repetition is allowed. Cryptographic arithmetic uses very large spaces, but a large number alone is not a security proof. The algorithm, assumptions, and adversary's abilities also matter.
M03.example: Compute 5×3 mod 7 = 1, so 3 is an inverse of 5 modulo 7. Compare this with 2 modulo 6: multiplying 2 by any integer cannot produce a remainder of 1. List the possible remainders to see why. Then count four-digit strings with and without repeated digits, explaining why the formulas differ.
M03.pitfall: Ordinary division cannot simply be copied into modular arithmetic. An inverse may not exist.

check.question: Does 2 have a multiplicative inverse modulo 6?
choices: Yes, every nonzero number has one for every modulus
Yes, its inverse is the decimal number 0.5
No, because 2 and 6 are not coprime
check.explanation: An inverse must be an integer residue whose product is 1 modulo 6. None exists because gcd(2,6)=2.

guide.bridge: From M03, count outcomes; from M01, interpret a fraction and percentage. For example, 3 of 10 is 3/10=0.3=30%. A percentage means “out of a hundred”. Readiness check: 20 of 1000 is 2%, not 20%.
guide.teaching:
Start with a collection you can count. If 3 of 10 equally likely cards are marked, the chance of selecting a marked card is 3/10. A probability is between 0 and 1: zero means impossible under the model and one means certain. The collection and the selection rule matter. Unequally likely cards need unequal weights rather than simply “favourable cards divided by all cards”.

Conditioning means keeping only cases where something is already known. P(A|B), read “probability of A given B”, asks what fraction of the B cases also have A. If we ask “of all alerts, which are real incidents?”, first gather the alerts, not the whole population. Reversing the question gives a different group: “of all real incidents, which caused an alert?”

Give the four cells names: a true positive (TP) is a real incident that alerted; a false positive (FP) is a benign event that alerted; a false negative (FN) is a missed incident; a true negative (TN) is a benign event that did not alert. Precision is TP divided by all alerts, TP+FP. Recall, also called sensitivity here, is TP divided by all incidents, TP+FN. Build these counts before reaching for a formula.

Probability assigns weights to an outcome space. Conditional probability P(A|B) asks about A after restricting attention to cases where B occurs. Independence means learning B does not change A's probability; it is an assumption to justify, not a synonym for events having different names.

A base rate is the frequency of the condition before considering a test. Even a sensitive detector can produce mostly false alarms when true incidents are rare. Use counts to avoid confusing P(alert|incident) with P(incident|alert). Precision asks what fraction of alerts are real; recall asks what fraction of real incidents alerted.

Entropy measures uncertainty under a distribution. For a fair bit it is one bit. Two equally likely independent bits have four equally likely outcomes and two bits of entropy. Four possible labels do not imply two bits if one label dominates. Predictable random-number seeds can make generated values unsuitable for security even when their printed distribution looks varied.

The formal conditional rule is \(P(A\mid B)=P(A\cap B)/P(B)\), for \(P(B)>0\). Bayes’ rule writes the same intersection in two ways: \(P(A\mid B)=P(B\mid A)P(A)/P(B)\). The denominator includes every way the observed event can happen; the alert table below makes that explicit. Independence is \(P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)\), including zero-probability cases without conditioning on them. Pairwise independence checks pairs; mutual independence requires the product rule for every subcollection. Neither should be assumed from a large sample alone. A discrete random variable assigns numbers to outcomes, and \(E[X]=\sum_x xP(X=x)\). Where expectations exist, \(E[X+Y]=E[X]+E[Y]\) even when \(X,Y\) are dependent. An expectation need not be an observed outcome. For a finite distribution, entropy is \(H(X)=-\sum_x p(x)\log_2 p(x)\), with zero-probability terms defined by their limiting value zero.
guide.example:
Population: 10,000 events
Real incidents: 100; benign: 9,900
Detector catches 90 incidents and alerts on 99 benign events.
                  alert  no alert
incident            90       10
benign              99     9801
Precision = 90/(90+99) ≈ 47.6%
Recall    = 90/(90+10) = 90%
guide.explanation: Read one row at a time. There are 100 real incidents: 90 alerted and 10 did not. There are 9,900 benign events: 99 alerted and 9,801 did not. The row totals add to 10,000, so no event is missing. The alert column has \(90+99=189\) events. Of those, 90 are true incidents, giving precision \(90/189\approx0.476=47.6\%\). For recall, keep the incident row: \(90/(90+10)=90\%\). The detector finds many incidents, yet more than half its alerts concern benign events. That happens because benign events are much more common. Choosing whether this burden is acceptable requires the costs of review and missed incidents, not a single “accuracy” slogan.
guide.exercise: Use a second population: 1,000 events, 20 incidents, 15 detected incidents and 35 false alerts. Fill all four matrix cells, calculate precision and recall, and state the number of missed incidents.
guide.solution: Start with the incident row: 20 incidents minus 15 detected gives 5 misses, so TP=15 and FN=5. There are \(1000-20=980\) benign events; subtract the 35 false alerts to get TN=945. All four cells sum to 1000. All alerts total \(15+35=50\), so precision is \(15/50=30\%\). All incidents total 20, so recall is \(15/20=75\%\). If your denominators are reversed, restate the question in words before recalculating.
guide.challenge: A detector is applied to 100 events, including 10 incidents. It catches 8 incidents and alerts on 18 benign events. Calculate precision, recall and total alerts. Explain why independent trials would be an unsafe assumption for repeated events from one device.
guide.challenge_solution: Precision=8/26≈30.8%; recall=80%; alerts=26. Events from one device may share configuration or a single incident and be correlated. Treating them as independent can overstate the amount of evidence.

M04.concept: Probability describes uncertainty under stated assumptions. Conditional probability asks about an event after learning another event occurred. Independence means learning one event does not change the probability of the other; it cannot be assumed just because two events have different names. Entropy measures uncertainty in a distribution, not the visual complexity of a string.
M04.mechanism: Security alerts must be interpreted alongside the base rate of actual incidents. A highly accurate detector can still produce mostly false alerts when malicious events are rare. Build a count table rather than relying on phrases such as '99% accurate'. Separate the true-positive rate from the probability that a positive result is malicious.
M04.example: Among 10,000 events, suppose 100 are malicious. A detector catches 90 and falsely flags 1% of 9,900 benign events: 99 false alerts. Of the 189 alerts, 90 are true positives, so precision is 90/189, approximately 47.6%. Recall asks about all 100 malicious events instead: 90/100=90%. Check each denominator and explain how the answer changes if the base rate changes.
M04.pitfall: A detector's sensitivity is not its precision. Both depend on which population and threshold are being measured.

check.question: In the worked example, approximately what fraction of alerts are true positives?
choices: About 47.6 percent
90 percent
99 percent
check.explanation: The current worked table has 90 true alerts and 99 false alerts. All alerts total 189, so precision is 90/189, about 47.6%. The 90% recall answers a different question.

guide.bridge: From M04, calculate precision and recall using all alerts and all incidents respectively. From M01, square a number by multiplying it by itself, and read sqrt(4)=2 as “which non-negative number squared gives 4?” We first describe three supplied measurements; only then discuss inference to a wider population.
guide.teaching:
Suppose three response times are 2, 4 and 6 milliseconds. Their mean is the sum divided by the count: (2+4+6)/3=4 ms. But another group of measurements could have the same mean and much more spread. A deviation is a measurement minus the mean: -2, 0, 2 here. Squaring gives 4, 0, 4, so negative and positive differences no longer cancel. The sample variance divides their sum by n-1: 8/2=4 square milliseconds. Its square root, the sample standard deviation, is 2 ms, back in the original unit. A millisecond is one thousandth of a second.

We have described the three measurements, not established how every future request behaves. A sample is what we observed; the population is what we hope to understand. If we measure only one unusually fast machine, collecting many readings there does not make that machine representative. Repeated readings from it may also be related rather than independent.

A population is the group you want to describe; a sample is what you measured. The mean is sum/n. Sample variance divides squared deviations by n-1 when estimating population variance under standard independent-sampling assumptions. Standard deviation returns to the original units; standard error describes uncertainty in an estimator, not variability among individual observations.

Imagine repeatedly drawing samples of the same size and computing their means. Those means have a sampling distribution. A normal distribution is a symmetric bell-shaped model described by a mean and standard deviation. Under appropriate conditions, averages can be approximately normal, but tiny, biased or strongly dependent samples do not become trustworthy just because a formula is available. With known population standard deviation sigma and a suitable normal model, a mean interval uses mean ±1.96*sigma/sqrt(n). When sigma is estimated, t methods and their assumptions matter instead.

A 95% confidence procedure covers the fixed population parameter in 95% of repeated samples under its assumptions. It is not a 95% probability that this particular fixed parameter moves inside this observed interval. A p-value concerns data at least as extreme under a null model, not the probability the null hypothesis is true. Choose metrics and splits before examining results, and preserve a held-out set against tuning.

sqrt(n) means the nonnegative square root of n: sqrt(100)=10 because 10×10=100. Squaring a deviation means multiplying it by itself. These operations explain the units in the worked variance and standard-error calculations.

A histogram groups measurements into bins and shows how many fall in each interval. With unequal bin widths, distinguish counts from a density plot whose bar areas represent proportions. A normal density is a bell-shaped model; probability is area over a range, not the curve’s height at a point. A fitted curve is an assumption to check, not a guarantee that counts, tail behaviour or new populations follow that model. Sampling with replacement means a selected observation stays eligible to be selected again; bootstrap resampling uses that operation on observed data and needs its own assumptions. More rows do not repair biased recruitment or dependence. Failure to reject a null does not establish equality or guarantee replication. The short replacement confidence-interval video illustrates repeated coverage; the formula and assumptions are worked below.

A held-out set is a collection reserved before tuning and used later to check a chosen method. If you repeatedly inspect it and change the method to improve its score, it is no longer an untouched final check. In this lesson’s core exercise, calculate the supplied summaries and identify the limits. Confidence intervals and p-values answer further inference questions and require the stated sampling model; work through their assigned reading before using them for a real study. In the known-sigma example, sigma=10 is a deliberately supplied population value, not a number learned from the three earlier observations.
guide.example:
Times (ms): 2, 4, 6
mean = 12/3 = 4
squared deviations = 4, 0, 4
sample variance = 8/(3-1) = 4 ms^2
sample standard deviation = 2 ms

Known-sigma teaching case:
mean=100, sigma=10, n=100
standard error=10/sqrt(100)=1
95% normal interval: [98.04, 101.96]
guide.explanation: The first calculation describes a tiny dataset and does not justify a population inference by itself. The second explicitly assumes a known sigma and an appropriate sampling model. Reusing sample standard deviation as if it were known population sigma hides uncertainty. Neither interval corrects a sample collected only from unusually fast machines.
guide.exercise: Calculate mean and sample variance for [1,3,5]. For TP=12,FP=3,FN=8,TN=77 calculate precision and recall. Write two reasons events collected repeatedly from one host might violate independent representative sampling.
guide.solution: For [1,3,5], the mean is \((1+3+5)/3=3\). Deviations from 3 are -2,0,2; their squares sum to 8. Sample variance is \(8/(3-1)=4\). The detection table has \(12+3=15\) alerts, so precision is \(12/15=80\%\); it has \(12+8=20\) incidents, so recall is \(12/20=60\%\). Repeated events from one host can share configuration and time-related causes. Observing just that host also limits which other hosts the conclusion can describe. State these as sampling limitations rather than treating additional decimal places as a remedy.
guide.challenge: Before comparing two synthetic rules, write a protocol: use the fixed matrix results A=(TP=18,FP=12,FN=2,TN=68), B=(TP=16,FP=4,FN=4,TN=76). Choose whether precision or recall matters more, calculate both and defend a choice. Critique “p=0.03 means the hypothesis is 97% likely true.”
guide.challenge_solution: A: precision60%,recall90%; B: precision80%,recall80%. A misses fewer incidents but produces more false alerts. Choice depends on declared costs, not a universally best score. A p-value is conditional on the null model and does not give its posterior probability. Include sampling unit, fixed held-out data and uncertainty limits in your protocol.

M05.concept: A sample is the data observed; a population is what you want to understand. Sampling bias arises when the selection process systematically excludes relevant cases. An average hides variation, so report distributions or suitable summaries alongside it. A confidence interval quantifies uncertainty under assumptions about how the data were produced; it does not repair biased measurement.
M05.mechanism: Experiments compare a treatment with a baseline while controlling alternative explanations. Decide the hypothesis, metrics, datasets, and stopping rule before looking for a favourable result. In detection work, precision asks how many alerts are correct; recall asks how many malicious events were found. A change can improve one while worsening the other.
M05.example: For a labelled set with 20 malicious events, a detector finds 15 and produces 5 false alerts. Compute recall as 15/20 and precision as 15/20. Now add 15 false alerts without changing the true positives: recall stays fixed while precision drops. Document the dataset's source and why its event mix may differ from production.
M05.pitfall: More decimal places do not mean greater certainty. Measurement quality and sample design determine what a result supports.

check.question: A detector finds the same malicious events but doubles its false alerts. What happens?
choices: Recall increases and precision stays the same
Recall stays the same and precision decreases
Both necessarily increase
check.explanation: Recall depends on true positives and missed malicious events. Extra false positives reduce precision without changing recall.

guide.bridge: From P01/P06, run a saved program and identify its input and output; from L01, use the shell and ./ to name a file in the current folder. From M01, recognise a byte and hex notation. Use the documented CS50 Linux environment or a configured local C compiler; check cc --version before this exercise. Windows learners should use the course Linux route for the shown shell commands.
guide.teaching:
In the earlier Python lessons, you gave a .py file to Python to run. For this C exercise, you first give a .c text file to a compiler, which builds a separate program you can run. Think of source as the instructions you wrote and the executable as the machine’s built version. Editing the source does not rebuild the executable automatically.

Read this tiny C skeleton before the numeric example: int main(void) names the starting function; { and } enclose its statements; a semicolon ends a statement; return 0 reports successful completion. #include <stdio.h> requests the declarations needed to use printf, which displays formatted output. These are C syntax rules, not Python indentation rules.

C source is text. A compiler translates it, and a linker resolves references to libraries to produce an executable. A syntax error stops translation; a runtime error happens after the program starts. Read compiler diagnostics rather than treating successful compilation as evidence of correct behaviour.

A type determines representation and permitted operations. Integer sizes depend on the type and implementation; do not assume every int is the same size everywhere. sizeof reports bytes for this implementation. Unsigned arithmetic wraps modulo one more than its maximum value; signed overflow is undefined behaviour, so it is not a portable wraparound technique.

Bytes have addresses and an order in memory. Endianness concerns the ordering of bytes within a multi-byte value, not the order in which you write ordinary decimal digits. Compile with warnings enabled and keep examples small enough to trace. Undefined behaviour can appear to work in one build, then change under optimisation; a single output is not a language guarantee.

The video uses the CS50 environment: make invokes configured build steps, and get_int/get_string plus the string alias come from its teaching library. They are not standard C functions or a built-in C string type. Our example needs only standard headers and the explicit cc command shown below. #include <stdio.h> supplies declarations and related definitions needed for the interface; the linker resolves the library implementation. Spell printf and stdio.h exactly, even when automatic captions distort them. ./sizes runs the executable in the current directory. After editing source, compile again before running; otherwise you may be observing an older executable.

A compact C syntax bridge: int main(void) defines the program’s entry function with no arguments here; braces enclose its body, semicolons finish statements, and return 0 reports success. A declaration names a variable and its type before use. printf has a format contract: %u expects an unsigned int and %zu expects size_t. Passing a different type can cause undefined behaviour. sizeof gives a count of C bytes; a byte is CHAR_BIT bits, at least eight, rather than universally eight. The byte-order drawing explicitly assumes eight-bit bytes and a two-byte value.

For integer operands, 1/3 is integer division and gives 0; casting an operand first, as in (double)1/3, requests floating-point division. Casting the already computed integer result is too late. A finite floating-point format approximates many values; printing more decimal places reveals that approximation rather than adding precision. Some applications instead use integer smallest units, exact fractions or suitable decimal arithmetic with an explicit rounding policy. The video’s type widths are examples from its environment, and its signed-overflow demonstration must not be copied as a portable guarantee.

Decode cc -std=c11 -Wall -Wextra sizes.c -o sizes: cc is the compiler driver; -std=c11 selects the C edition used by this example; -Wall and -Wextra request useful warnings; sizes.c is the source; -o sizes names the executable. Run ./sizes only after compilation succeeds. If cc is missing, use the documented setup rather than changing source to hide the error. In the example UINT_MAX is a named limit supplied by limits.h. sizeof(int) asks this implementation for the storage size, and %zu tells printf how to display that size value. Trace one line at a time instead of treating punctuation as magic.
guide.explanation: UINT_MAX is the implementation's largest unsigned int. Adding unsigned 1 wraps to zero by the language rule. The %zu conversion matches sizeof's size_t type. Replacing the unsigned variable with a maximum signed int and overflowing it would remove the portable guarantee; do not infer signed behaviour from this result.
guide.exercise: Compile the supplied program and record compiler version, command, warnings and output. Draw how the number 0x0102 would occupy two bytes under little-endian and big-endian conventions. Do not claim sizeof(int) is universal.
guide.solution: Little-endian: lower address 02 then 01; big-endian: 01 then 02. Unsigned wrap prints zero. The observed size belongs to the recorded platform.
guide.challenge: Explain each stage from source to execution. In an explicitly eight-bit unsigned mathematical model calculate 250+10. Then explain why this is not a general prediction for an expression involving signed char in a real C program.
guide.challenge_solution: The fixed-width unsigned model gives 260 mod256=4. In real C, narrow integer operands normally undergo integer promotion before arithmetic; storing an out-of-range result in signed char is a conversion question, whose rules depend on the C edition and implementation. It is not automatically signed arithmetic overflow. Arithmetic overflow in a signed operation such as INT_MAX+1 is undefined. Separate the mathematical model, operand promotions, conversion rules and recorded compiler behaviour.

C01.concept: C makes the relationship between source code and machine execution more visible. A compiler translates source into object code, and a linker combines objects and libraries into an executable. Types determine how values are represented and which operations are meaningful. A declaration is a promise to the compiler, not automatic validation of external input.
C01.mechanism: Integer widths and signedness matter. Unsigned arithmetic wraps modulo a power of two; signed overflow in C is undefined behaviour. Undefined behaviour means the language does not promise a particular result, so an observed wraparound cannot be relied upon. Enable compiler warnings and understand each warning before treating a successful build as correct execution.
C01.example: Compile a program that prints sizeof values for selected integer types and reports the limits from the standard headers. Compare a safe boundary calculation with an intentionally avoided overflowing expression. Record compiler version and flags. Explain which observations come from this platform and which properties come from the language specification.
C01.pitfall: A program compiling without errors does not prove memory safety or correct arithmetic.

check.question: May portable C code rely on signed integer overflow wrapping around?
choices: Yes; all C integers wrap identically
Yes; a successful compilation guarantees it
No; signed overflow has undefined behaviour
check.explanation: Unsigned wrapping is defined, but signed overflow is undefined. Optimisations may assume it never happens.

guide.bridge: From C01, save, compile and run a C program. From M01, distinguish text from the bytes used to store it. An array is an ordered group of slots; its first index is 0, as in the Python list examples. Today’s pointer notation is explained as a short bridge before C04.
guide.teaching:
Picture four numbered boxes: 0, 1, 2, 3. char dst[4] reserves four char slots. A buffer is simply storage reserved for data; its capacity is how much it can hold. To store the C string "cat", put c in box 0, a in 1, t in 2 and a zero terminator in 3. That final byte tells C string functions where the text stops. It is not the printed digit '0'; '\0' denotes the zero character value.

An array is a contiguous sequence of elements. For char name[4], valid indices are 0 through 3. A C string additionally needs a zero byte marking its end. Three visible characters plus the terminator fill four bytes; the terminator is data occupying a real position.

An array does not carry a universal runtime bounds check. A function receiving a pointer generally needs a separate capacity contract. Reading beyond the last element is a defect even when it does not immediately crash. Distinguish input byte count, allocated capacity and visible character count, especially when using UTF-8.

A safe interface checks available capacity before copying and reports failure explicitly. Truncation is not always acceptable: truncating an identifier could select a different account or resource. Decide whether to reject, truncate or resize based on the application's meaning. Do not use a successful print as proof that the buffer was large enough.

Syntax bridge before the deeper pointer lesson: const char *src declares a pointer through which characters are read without modification. Here it refers to the first character of the valid string literal "cat". It is not a second copy of the text. char dst[4] allocates four character slots; sizeof dst measures that array’s full byte capacity here. In most expressions an array converts to a pointer to its first element. A pointer variable does not carry the original array length, so sizeof on a pointer in a helper function would measure the pointer, not the source or destination buffer. C04 explains addresses and pointer operations further.

An indexed loop can be written for (size_t i = 0; i < count; i++) { /* use items[i] */ }. Initialisation happens once, the condition is checked before each iteration, and i++ runs after the body. A function prototype tells the compiler the argument and return types before a call; the body supplies the implementation. An array/length pair is a contract the caller must honour. For the lecture’s average, length must be positive and no greater than the available elements; accumulating arbitrary integers can overflow. A return type of float does not undo integer division already performed inside the expression.

strlen returns size_t and counts bytes before the first zero, not allocated capacity or user-perceived characters. memcpy copies exactly the requested byte count and does not add a terminator; the +1 below intentionally copies the existing zero. Its source/destination must be valid for that count and must not overlap. ASCII itself defines values 0–127; a common eight-bit byte can hold more values, but that does not make them all ASCII.
guide.explanation: The comparison rejects a source whose visible byte length leaves no room for the terminator. Copying strlen+1 includes the terminator. This small example assumes src is already a valid terminated string; strlen itself cannot safely validate an arbitrary unterminated buffer.
guide.exercise: Save the example as strings.c. Compile with cc -std=c11 -Wall -Wextra strings.c -o strings, then run ./strings. On the next terminal line, run printf 'status=%s\n' "$?" to display that run’s exit status; run no other command between them. Repeat after changing src to "cats", then to "", recompiling each time. Predict the displayed text and status first. Draw the occupied indices for accepted inputs, including the terminator. The rejected case prints no text; the status is how it reports refusal.
guide.solution: With "cat", the program prints cat and returns status 0; indices 0–3 contain c,a,t and the terminator. With "cats", strlen is 4, so 4>=4 is true and return 1 stops before copying; status is 1. With "", strlen is 0; copying 0+1 byte stores just the terminator at index 0, then printf displays an empty line and the program returns 0. The remaining array bytes are not part of that empty string. None of these cases needs access beyond dst[3].
guide.challenge: A destination has capacity 6 bytes. Decide whether ASCII inputs "hello", "planet" and "" fit as terminated strings. Explain why a five-character Unicode string may still fail this byte-capacity check.
guide.challenge_solution: hello fits exactly with its terminator; planet needs7 bytes and is rejected; empty needs1. UTF-8 characters can occupy multiple bytes, so visible character count does not establish byte length.

C02.concept: An array stores a fixed sequence of elements. A C string convention uses a zero byte to mark its end; the terminator occupies space too. An array of four bytes can hold three single-byte characters plus a terminator. Text encodings complicate length: a character perceived by a reader need not occupy one byte.
C02.mechanism: A buffer's capacity, the number of bytes currently used, and the length of decoded text are different quantities. Check bounds before writing and account for terminators and encoding expansion. A function receiving a pointer cannot usually infer the original array's capacity, so pass sizes explicitly and document whether a size includes the terminator.
C02.example: Draw a four-cell buffer containing c, a, t, and zero. Attempting to append another character requires a fifth cell for a new terminator. Rewrite the operation to check required capacity before modifying anything. Repeat with a non-ASCII UTF-8 word and count bytes separately from displayed characters.
C02.pitfall: A null terminator is a byte value, not the same concept as a null pointer. Confusing the two leads to incorrect boundary reasoning.

check.question: How much capacity does the C string "cat" require with its terminator?
choices: At least four bytes
Exactly three bytes
One pointer-sized cell regardless of contents
check.explanation: Three character bytes plus the terminating zero byte require four bytes.

guide.bridge: Builds on C02 arrays and M02 graphs/proofs. Trace by hand first; Python may be used for the bounded implementation.
guide.teaching:
Imagine finding a word in an alphabetically ordered index. A linear search checks entries in sequence. Binary search checks the middle and uses the ordering to discard a part that cannot contain the answer. Without the ordering rule, that discard is unjustified. An algorithm is the procedure; a data structure is how the entries and relationships are stored.

For simple structures, trace the removal rule. Push A then B onto a stack and remove B first, like the top plate of a pile. Put A then B into a queue and remove A first, like the front of a waiting line. A tree has parent–child relationships, like folders and subfolders. These analogies explain order or shape; they do not establish permissions, memory layout or actual speed.

An algorithm specifies steps; a data structure determines how information is organised for those steps. A list scan can inspect every item, while a sorted array permits binary search. Faster lookup can require more costly updates or stronger assumptions, so complexity belongs to a particular operation and representation.

A recursive function solves a problem by calling itself on smaller instances. It needs a base case and a measure that decreases toward it. Each call has its own local state. Draw calls and returns separately: a recursive definition does not execute every line at once.

Big-O describes an asymptotic upper bound, not an exact runtime. Linear search uses at most n comparisons; repeatedly halving a sorted search interval needs on the order of log2(n). Constants, allocation and cache effects still matter in real measurements. First prove that the algorithm returns the correct result under its input assumptions; an incorrect fast result is not an optimisation.

Write the cost function before its bound: worst-case comparisons, best-case comparisons and allocated bytes are different functions. For nonnegative costs, \(f(n)\in O(g(n))\) means there are fixed \(c>0\) and \(n_0\) such that \(f(n)\le c g(n)\) for every \(n\ge n_0\). Omega reverses the inequality; Theta requires both bounds for the same function. For \(f(n)=3n+7\), choose \(c=10,n_0=1\) to prove \(O(n)\); it is also \(O(n^2)\), so an upper bound need not be tight. A finite ratio limit can establish a bound when it exists, but a convergent ratio is not required by the definition.

Selection sort repeatedly moves the smallest remaining item into the next final position. Its remaining-suffix scans total \((n-1)+(n-2)+\cdots+1=n(n-1)/2\) comparisons in the usual implementation. Merge sort instead sorts two smaller halves and merges them: merging two sorted arrays advances one input pointer per output item, taking linear work. There are about \(\log_2 n\) merge levels, each with linear total work, giving \(\Theta(n\log n)\) for the ordinary implementation and \(O(n)\) auxiliary array space. Recursion stack depth and auxiliary array capacity are distinct costs. Hash tables provide expected constant-time lookup under stated hashing/load assumptions; collisions can make a lookup linear. A balanced search tree can provide logarithmic lookup; an unbalanced chain cannot. A Python list is an array-like sequence, not a linked list.

Read the worked search as a boundary problem. lo is the first possible insertion position; hi is the last possible boundary and is excluded from the entries inspected. [lo,hi) is shorthand for “include lo, stop before hi”. With four items, indices are 0–3, but insertion after the last item is position 4. // performs whole-number floor division. The loop ends when the two boundaries meet, even if the target is absent. We then return the position, not True or False.
guide.explanation: For target 5 in [1,3,5,7], begin lo=0, hi=4. First mid=(0+4)//2=2, where the value is 5. It is not less than the target, so hi becomes 2. Next mid=(0+2)//2=1, where 3 is less than 5, so lo becomes 2. Now lo=hi=2 and the loop stops. Position 2 is the first place whose value is at least 5. For a missing target such as 6, position 3 is still meaningful: insert there to retain order. To claim membership, additionally check index < len(items) before reading items[index], then check equality. The short-circuit order prevents reading position 4 when insertion is after the last item.
guide.exercise: Trace the exact function for targets 0,5,6,9 and input [1,3,5,7], plus an empty list. Record every interval and final insertion index.
guide.solution: Indices are0,2,3,4; empty returns 0. The interval shrinks on every iteration. Searching unsorted input invalidates the reasoning even if one target happens to work.
guide.challenge: Implement recursive sum_list(items,index=0) with an empty-suffix base case. Trace [2,4,6], count additions and explain time and call-stack growth. State an input size limitation of recursion in Python.

C03.concept: An algorithm's cost describes how its work grows as input grows. Linear search may inspect every item, while binary search repeatedly halves an ordered search space. Big-O notation describes an asymptotic bound; it does not promise an exact runtime or account for every constant factor. State the operation being counted and assumptions about the input.
C03.mechanism: Stacks remove the most recently added item; queues remove the earliest. Trees encode hierarchical relationships. Learn these abstract behaviours before implementing pointer-based structures. Recursion solves a problem through smaller instances and needs a base case plus progress toward it. Each recursive call also consumes execution resources.
C03.example: Search a sorted list of sixteen values by repeatedly selecting a midpoint and discarding the impossible half. Write the remaining interval after each comparison. Then trace recursive factorial for 3 down to its base case and back up. Explain why the binary search needs sorted input, while the factorial recursion needs a decreasing nonnegative argument.
C03.pitfall: A theoretically faster algorithm may be slower on tiny inputs. Measure relevant workloads after establishing correctness.

check.question: Which prerequisite makes ordinary binary search correct?
choices: The list contains an even number of items
The search interval is ordered according to the comparison rule
Every value is stored as text
check.explanation: The decision to discard half the interval depends on its ordering. Without that property, the target could be discarded.

guide.bridge: From C02, tell an array’s capacity from a string’s length. From C01, compile and run C; from C03, draw a node and arrow. First distinguish “the address of a box” from “the number stored in the box”. The exercise deliberately runs only valid accesses.
guide.teaching:
Use a paper box labelled x containing 7. The box has a location, or address. A pointer p stores that address rather than the number 7 itself. &x asks for the address; *p asks for the object at the address p stores. In a declaration, int *p says “p is a pointer to int”; in an expression, *p accesses its pointed-to int. The same symbol appears in different grammatical roles. Copying p into q makes two arrows to the same box, not two boxes.

A pointer stores an address. &x obtains an address; *p accesses the object at the address when p is valid. A pointer's type helps determine how dereferencing and pointer arithmetic behave. It does not prove the referenced object is still alive or within bounds.

Automatic local objects commonly live in a stack frame, while malloc allocates storage whose lifetime must be managed explicitly. These are useful implementation pictures, but object lifetime is the language-level rule that matters. Returning the address of a local variable leaves a dangling pointer after the function returns. Freeing a heap allocation ends its usable lifetime even if the old bytes remain visible.

Track ownership: who allocates, who may use an object and who must free it exactly once. A linked node contains data and a pointer to another node; draw both the node and the arrow. Distinguish pointer variable, pointed-to object and the value inside that object. A debugger can inspect these locations, but its displayed addresses vary between runs.

C passes every argument by value. Passing &x copies a pointer value, and dereferencing that copy can modify x while x is alive. This is different from introducing a separate reference-parameter feature. For a struct pointer p, p->next means (*p).next; parentheses matter. A self-referential declaration can use typedef struct node { int number; struct node *next; } node;. The compiler may insert alignment padding, so allocate sizeof *p rather than adding guessed field sizes.

Pointer size, printed representation and stack direction are platform details. NULL denotes a null pointer constant/interface value; its internal representation is not universally all-zero bytes. A valid pointer is more than an arbitrary integer address: bounds, alignment, object type and lifetime matter. Pointer arithmetic is limited to the relevant array object and its one-past position; that one-past pointer cannot be dereferenced. malloc returns uninitialised storage or a failure indication; it is an allocator API, not necessarily one OS call per request.

An exhausted call stack is a resource-limit failure. A stack-buffer overflow writes past a buffer in stack storage, and a heap-buffer overflow writes past an allocated heap buffer. These are distinct from a memory leak or a use-after-free. Valgrind or a sanitizer can expose defects on exercised paths, but passing one run is not a proof over all inputs. The core exercise compiles as cc -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -pedantic memory.c -o memory, then ./memory; a nonzero allocation-failure return is an explicit outcome. Do not execute the invalid accesses in the paper questions.

Now trace the supplied allocation. malloc asks for storage; sizeof *p supplies enough for one object of the pointed-to type without guessing its byte count. For this non-variable-length int type, sizeof does not dereference an uninitialised p. If allocation fails, p equals NULL and the program returns before using it. *p = 7 writes the new object’s value; q = p copies the address; *q reads the same 7. free(p) releases that allocation. p = NULL and q = NULL overwrite the local arrow variables; they do not revive the released object or update aliases elsewhere. Draw the lifetime ending as well as the arrows changing.
guide.explanation: p and q are two variables referring to one allocation. Freeing p does not automatically reset q. Setting p to NULL alone cannot repair every alias; the program must ensure all uses stop. The diagram shows why copying a pointer does not copy its target. malloc failure is checked before dereference.
guide.exercise: Compile and run the safe example. Draw the pointer/object diagram after allocation, after q=p and after free. Without executing invalid access, explain what would be wrong with printing *q after free or freeing q as well.
guide.solution: The safe output is 7. After free, dereferencing q is use-after-free and freeing it again is a double-free defect. Resetting aliases in this small scope makes subsequent accidental use easier to detect but is not a general ownership system.
guide.challenge: Draw two linked nodes holding 10 and20, with first.next pointing to second and second.next null. Describe an order for freeing both without reading an already-freed node.
guide.challenge_solution: Save the next pointer before freeing the current node, or free the known second node before the first in this two-node case. A traversal must not dereference first.next after first has been freed. Explain allocation-failure handling and exactly-one-free ownership.

C04.concept: A pointer stores an address. Dereferencing accesses the object at that address, provided the object exists and access is valid. Stack allocation commonly follows function-call lifetimes; dynamically allocated heap objects live until released. A pointer may still hold an address after an object's lifetime ends, creating a dangling pointer.
C04.mechanism: Ownership answers who must release an allocation and when other code may use it. Linked structures connect separately allocated nodes through pointers, so freeing a node requires preserving the next link before the node becomes invalid. A memory leak loses access to allocated memory; use-after-free accesses memory after release. These are different defects.
C04.example: Draw two linked nodes with addresses, values, and next pointers. Walk from the head, saving next before freeing the current node. After the walk, set the head to null. Use a debugger or memory diagnostic on a small local implementation and compare its report with your ownership diagram rather than guessing from a crash alone.
C04.pitfall: Setting one pointer to null does not invalidate other aliases that still point to the released object.

check.question: Why is dereferencing an old alias unsafe after its allocation is freed?
choices: Free automatically updates every alias to null
Heap addresses are always immediately erased
The object's lifetime has ended even if the address value remains
check.explanation: The pointer value can outlive the object. Access through it is invalid regardless of whether bytes still appear unchanged.

guide.bridge: From C04, distinguish an address from the value stored there; from C01, compile a source file; from M01, recognise bits and bytes. A register is a small named storage location built into the processor. This lesson compares two illustrative conventions rather than assuming every learner uses the same CPU.
guide.teaching:
Start with add(3,4). The source-level question is simple: pass two numbers to a function and return 7. The machine must agree on where those numbers are placed and where the caller should look for the answer. A calling convention is that agreement. Registers are named processor storage locations, and an instruction is one operation on values or control flow. Assembly gives those operations readable names.

An instruction set defines machine operations; a calling convention defines how functions exchange arguments, results and preserved state. Under x86-64 System V, early integer arguments use registers such as rdi and rsi, and integer results use rax. This is a platform convention, not a universal property of functions.

An executable also contains sections and metadata for loading. A disassembler interprets bytes as instructions; a debugger observes a running process. Source lines and instructions do not map one-to-one after optimisation. Compiler-generated code may eliminate a variable or inline a function while preserving defined observable behaviour.

To trace a function, record the input registers, each value-changing instruction and the output. Keep addresses separate from values stored at those addresses. Use a tiny program with known source and no external input first. If your CPU is ARM, inspect its compiler output and consult the assigned architecture material rather than pretending the x86 register names apply.

The video’s eip/esp/ebp model is 32-bit x86. The native rdi/rsi/rax example is the separate x86-64 System V ABI. Do not mix their argument locations or pointer widths. In AT&T syntax, addl $8, %eax changes eax from 3 to 11; in Intel syntax the operand order and notation differ. If four bytes at increasing addresses are 11 22 33 44 hexadecimal, their 32-bit little-endian value is 0x44332211. Registers hold values; parentheses in the displayed AT&T memory operand request a memory access through an address.

For an ordinary x86 call, call records a return address and transfers control; ret retrieves where to resume. The numerical function result uses the ABI’s result location, not that return-address slot. A prologue may save a frame pointer and reserve local storage; an epilogue reverses the required state changes. A compiler can omit the frame pointer, inline the function or put variables in registers. Static storage duration means lifetime through the execution, not that a variable is immutable. The lecture’s fixed local-variable ordering is an examination convention, not a general C layout rule. Read the function-call section after the video because the recording explicitly defers that part.

Read a tiny illustrative x86-64 System V sequence in AT&T syntax: movl %edi, %eax copies the first int argument, 3, to the result register; addl %esi, %eax adds the second argument, 4, giving 7; ret returns control to the caller. AT&T writes source before destination. For an illustrative AArch64 integer call, w0 holds the first int and also the int result, and w1 the second int. add w0, w0, w1 replaces w0 with their sum; ret returns control. This syntax writes the destination first. These examples explain data movement; your compiler may generate a longer sequence. Neither return instruction is itself the number 7.
guide.explanation: cc -S emits assembly without executing it. -O0 makes the source relationship easier to observe, although the compiler may still choose its own sequence. A stored return address records where control resumes; it is not the function's numerical return value. Record CPU, OS and compiler before comparing your output with a lecture.
guide.exercise: First annotate the supplied illustrative three-step x86 trace or two-step AArch64 trace on paper: inputs, arithmetic result and control return. Then save add.c and run cc -S -O0 add.c -o add.s in your configured compiler environment. -S emits assembly text; it does not run the function. Record your CPU/compiler and find the arithmetic operation. Change + to -, save as subtract.c and generate a second .s file. Compare the operation with the predicted 3-4=-1. If argument locations differ from the illustrations, use the assigned platform material and record the difference rather than forcing a match. A zero-argument executable is not needed to inspect these function bodies.
guide.solution: The first function computes3+4=7 and the modified one3-4=-1. A correct annotation explains actual register/stack locations from the selected platform; matching a memorised x86 listing is not required.
guide.challenge: Explain the difference among an instruction-set register, a source variable, a return address and a return value. Predict add(8,-2) and state why compiler optimisation may change the instruction listing without changing that defined result.
guide.challenge_solution: The result is 6. Variables are source abstractions; registers are architectural storage; return address is control-flow metadata; return value is data passed back by convention. Optimisations may fold or inline the computation while preserving its defined behaviour.

C05.concept: Machine instructions operate on registers, memory, and control flow. Assembly is a readable notation for those instructions. A calling convention specifies how arguments, return values, and preserved registers cross function boundaries. An executable format such as ELF describes code, data, and metadata used by the operating system's loader.
C05.mechanism: A debugger connects source-level intentions with machine state. Breakpoints pause execution; stepping advances it; register and memory views expose values. Optimised builds may rearrange or remove source operations, so use a simple debug build first and then compare optimisation effects. An address seen in one run is not necessarily stable in another.
C05.example: Compile a tiny function that adds two integers with debug information. Break at its entry, inspect the argument locations for your platform's calling convention, step through the addition, and inspect the return value. Disassemble the function and map each relevant instruction to the source operation. Record architecture and compiler flags with the evidence.
C05.pitfall: Assembly syntax and calling conventions vary by architecture and platform. Do not apply an x86-64 register rule to every system.

check.question: What does a calling convention define?
choices: How functions exchange arguments, results, and register responsibilities
Which password a debugger requires
The trustworthiness of an executable's author
check.explanation: A calling convention is an interface agreement for machine-level function calls, not an authenticity check.

guide.bridge: Builds on C04 object lifetime, L02 permissions and C05 execution. Observe only your own processes and files.
guide.teaching:
Your text editor, browser and other programs share one computer. The operating system, or OS, coordinates their use of processors, memory, files and devices. It gives a running program a process context and checks requests to protected resources. The kernel is the privileged core of that OS. An application normally asks the kernel to open a file rather than directly controlling the storage device.

An address is like a numbered location inside a particular map. Two separate buildings can both have a room 12; equal room numbers do not make them the same room. Similarly, two processes can both use virtual address 0x1000 while their mappings refer to different physical memory. This analogy explains the need for a map; actual page permissions and mapping rules are enforced by the hardware/OS, not by the written address alone.

A process has an execution context and an address-space view; a thread is an execution path within a process. Virtual memory maps process-visible addresses to underlying storage, so equal-looking virtual addresses in two processes need not refer to the same physical memory.

User mode limits what ordinary instructions may do. A system call enters the kernel to request services such as opening a file. The kernel checks relevant credentials and object permissions. A library function can wrap a system call, but not every function call enters the kernel. Page protection also distinguishes readable, writable and executable mappings.

A filesystem maps names to objects and metadata. A file descriptor refers to an open-file interface, not merely a filename string. Renaming or unlinking a path does not necessarily terminate an already-open descriptor. Trace identity, name resolution, permission checks and object lifetime separately when explaining access.

Keep account privilege separate from CPU mode: an administrator’s program normally executes in user mode and enters kernel mode through controlled mechanisms. The trusted computing base consists of components relied upon to enforce the policy; a failure inside it can undermine that policy. Reducing it is useful, but size alone does not prove correctness. The video’s 4 KiB mapping is one hardware example. File descriptors refer to opened objects, whereas pathnames require lookup. Journaling records selected filesystem updates for crash recovery; it does not promise every application write is atomic, durable or backed up. An application may need a documented write/flush/rename protocol under the specific filesystem contract.
guide.example:
Own process A          Own process B
virtual address 0x1000  virtual address 0x1000
      |                       |
 mapping A                mapping B
      v                       v
 physical page X          physical page Y

Read path:
program -> open(path) -> kernel permission check -> descriptor
program -> read(descriptor) -> bytes or error
guide.explanation: The diagram explains isolation, not a promise that these exact addresses exist. A shared-memory mapping can deliberately make two processes access the same underlying page. File mode checks depend on the process identity and path traversal, so a filename alone is not enough to determine the result.
guide.exercise:
Use a fresh os-lab directory under your learning folder. Run each line below individually and inspect failures before continuing. If os-lab already exists, choose a different unused practice name throughout.

```sh
mkdir os-lab
chmod 700 os-lab
printf 'fictional practice note\n' > os-lab/note.txt
chmod 600 os-lab/note.txt
id
ls -ld os-lab
ls -l os-lab/note.txt
cat os-lab/note.txt
```

Record what id reports about your current identity, what the directory and file mode listings show, and the text read back. Draw program → open request → kernel checks → open descriptor → read. Label the command outputs as observations; the internal request path is an explanation based on the OS model, not something those commands directly traced. Do not infer that a privileged administrator could not read the note.
guide.solution: The read-back text is fictional practice note. id identifies the account running the commands and its groups. The mode listing normally shows rwx------ for the directory (700) and rw------- for the file (600), with possible additional platform indicators. Reading the file requires a reachable path and file-read permission for that identity. The successful cat is evidence that this read succeeded; it does not show every kernel operation or prove isolation against every other account. Both the observed settings and their stated limits belong in your answer.
guide.challenge: Two processes each print an identical virtual pointer value. Is that sufficient to prove shared memory? Explain what mapping evidence would be required. Separately explain why a library call and a system call are different concepts.
guide.challenge_solution: Identical virtual values do not prove shared backing. You need explicit shared mappings or equivalent OS evidence. A library routine executes user-space code and may invoke zero, one or several system calls.

C06.concept: The operating system manages processes, memory, devices, and files. User mode restricts what an ordinary process can do directly; system calls request controlled kernel operations. Virtual memory gives each process an address-space view that maps to physical memory and other backing storage. An address is meaningful in its process and mapping context.
C06.mechanism: A filesystem maps names to stored objects and metadata. An open file descriptor refers to an opened resource, which may outlive a filename change. Access checks, process identities, and kernel enforcement work together. Isolation reduces interference, but privileged components and shared resources remain important parts of the trust boundary.
C06.example: Run a harmless program that opens a file, reads bytes, and closes it. Observe its system calls using the supplied course tooling. Draw the path from application request to kernel check to returned data. Compare two processes' address maps and explain why equal-looking virtual addresses need not refer to the same physical bytes.
C06.pitfall: User-space checks cannot replace a required kernel or server-side enforcement boundary. A caller may bypass the intended interface.

check.question: Why can two processes use the same virtual address without sharing that memory?
choices: Virtual addresses are globally unique across all processes
Their address spaces can map it to different physical pages
Equal addresses always prove a shared secret
check.explanation: Virtual memory mappings are process-specific. The same numeric address may identify unrelated physical pages.

guide.bridge: From P02, trace one assignment at a time; from M02, explain a property that should remain true after each permitted action. From C06, distinguish a process from a thread. Today you draw schedules on paper, so no timing-dependent code or extra software is needed.
guide.teaching:
Concurrency means multiple activities can overlap in progress. A high-level statement such as counter=counter+1 can contain a read, arithmetic and write. Interleaving those pieces can lose an update even if each individual read and write succeeds.

A critical section protects the state transition that must appear indivisible to competing activities. Both writers must follow the same locking protocol. Locking only the write after an unprotected read is insufficient because the decision already used stale state. An invariant states what must remain true, such as each accepted reservation reducing available stock exactly once.

Deadlock can occur when activities wait cyclically for resources. A consistent lock order helps prevent that pattern. A race that does not happen in one test has not been disproved: thread scheduling changes across runs and systems. Reason about allowed schedules in addition to running tests.

Concurrency is overlapping progress; parallelism is simultaneous execution. A process owns an execution context and address space; threads in one process normally share that process’s memory. Shared-memory communication therefore needs an explicit coordination protocol. In the video, LD means read/load and ST means write/store. A circular buffer of capacity N wraps its next index from N-1 back to zero using (index + 1) % N.

In the videos’ abstract semaphore, WAIT atomically waits for an available count and decrements it; SIGNAL returns or supplies a count. Initialise CHARS to zero and SPACES to N. A producer first reserves a space, writes an item, then signals an item; a consumer reserves an item, reads it, then signals a space. These availability counters do not by themselves protect shared indices from multiple writers. Add the appropriate shared lock around those updates, and do not wait for availability while holding the lock needed by another participant to make that availability change.

Atomic under a lock means other participants following the same protocol cannot enter the protected operation concurrently. It does not mean the operating system cannot interrupt or schedule away the holder. A real withdrawal must protect the sufficient-funds check and the debit together. Locks do not provide persistence, crash recovery or rollback; database transactions have additional guarantees. Deadlock prevention by a global lock order requires all participating paths to obey it and does not guarantee fair scheduling or absence of starvation.
guide.example:
Initial counter=0
Step   Thread A       Thread B       shared
1      read -> a=0                   0
2                     read -> b=0   0
3      write a+1                     1
4                     write b+1     1

Desired serial result: 2
Repair: lock; read+add+write; unlock (in BOTH threads).
guide.explanation: Each thread calculated from the same old value. The second write replaced1 with 1, so one increment disappeared. Protecting the full read-modify-write makes one thread observe the other's completed update. A separate lock object per thread would not coordinate them.
guide.exercise: Draw an interleaving that correctly ends at 2 without a lock and the failing schedule above. Then draw both possible serial lock-protected orders. Explain why seeing2 in a test does not establish race freedom.
guide.solution: Unlocked A-read/A-write/B-read/B-write ends2; the supplied overlap ends1. Both protected serial orders end2. The test observes only sampled schedules, while the failure is allowed under a different interleaving.
guide.challenge: Task A acquires lock X then Y; task B acquires Y then X. Draw the point at which each holds one lock while waiting for the other, so neither can continue. Change both to acquire X before Y and explain which circular-wait pattern this prevents. Does that ordering alone guarantee correct account balances, fair scheduling or recovery after a crash? Explain one problem with holding a lock during slow input/output.
guide.challenge_solution: Schedule: A acquires X; B acquires Y; A waits for Y; B waits for X. Requiring both to acquire X before Y prevents this cycle: whichever task lacks X must wait before it can acquire Y. Release locks reliably. This ordering does not by itself protect a balance update, prove fair scheduling or make data durable after a crash. The data operation still needs the correct common critical section. Holding a lock across slow input/output delays other users of that lock and can create a long stall even without circular waiting.

C07.concept: Concurrency means tasks can make progress during overlapping periods. A race occurs when correctness depends on an uncontrolled ordering of accesses. A critical section groups operations that must not interleave in a harmful way. A lock can enforce mutual exclusion when every relevant participant follows the same locking protocol.
C07.mechanism: Locks do not automatically preserve a larger invariant. A check followed by a later update can still race if the lock covers only one part. Deadlock occurs when tasks wait on one another and none can progress. Consistent lock ordering is one way to prevent circular waiting; smaller shared state and clearer ownership often simplify the problem.
C07.example: Two threads each read balance=10, subtract 7, and write 3. Both report success even though only one withdrawal should have been permitted. Draw that interleaving. Then protect the check and update together, so the second operation sees balance=3 and fails. Explain the invariant: accepted withdrawals must not make the balance negative.
C07.pitfall: A sleep changes timing but does not establish synchronisation. A race disappearing during debugging may still exist.

check.question: Which region must be atomic for a guarded withdrawal?
choices: Only printing the receipt
Only reading the account's display name
Checking the balance and committing the debit together
check.explanation: The decision and its state update must share one protected operation. Separating them leaves an interleaving window.

guide.bridge: Builds on C06 processes and M01 units. Use the supplied message trace before installing packet tools.
guide.teaching:
Start with two computers exchanging a request and reply. A protocol is an agreed set of rules for the messages: their format, meaning and permitted order. Each end of a conversation is an endpoint. A router forwards traffic toward another network; a hop is one step along the route. Instead of making one mechanism solve every problem, networks divide responsibilities into layers.

Use an addressed parcel as a limited analogy. The contents are the payload; extra information used to deliver or interpret them is a header. An application supplies the useful message.
