A transport protocol manages a conversation between applications. IP handles delivery across networks, and a link protocol carries a frame over the next local step. Adding a wrapper is encapsulation. The analogy explains responsibilities, but packet delivery can split, repeat or reorder pieces, unlike one intact parcel. An application message is not necessarily one packet.

A network protocol defines message meaning and exchange rules. Layering separates concerns: link delivery on a local segment, IP forwarding across networks, transport behaviour between endpoints and application meaning. A packet capture observes data at a particular location, not every event in the entire network.

An application message can span several packets, and one packet may contain only part of the message. Encapsulation adds headers around data. Addresses at different layers identify different things: a local link address is not the same as an IP address or application hostname.

Latency is elapsed time; throughput is data per unit time; loss counts data not delivered under the measurement definition. Always include units and direction. A fast link can still have high round-trip latency. If a capture begins after a connection starts, missing setup packets are a visibility limitation rather than proof that no setup occurred.

Transmission time for a packet of \(L\) bits on a link of \(R\) bits per second is \(L/R\) seconds. Convert units first: 1500 bytes is 12000 bits, so at 1 megabit/second transmission takes 12 ms. Propagation depends on path length and signal speed, not packet size. Buffering adds variable queue delay; finite queues can drop arrivals. A traceroute hop value is a round-trip measurement, with possible filtering and rate limits, not that link’s one-way delay. The video’s technology speeds and operator names describe its recording era. RFCs include different document categories; IEEE, IETF and W3C all contribute relevant standards.
guide.example:
Application: request "hello"
Transport: TCP carries a byte stream
Network: IP forwards packets toward destination
Link: local frame reaches next hop

Teaching timing:
send at 0 ms; response at 80 ms
payload delivered: 1,000,000 bytes in 2 seconds
RTT=80 ms; throughput=500,000 bytes/s=4,000,000 bits/s
guide.explanation: The request leaves at 0 ms and its reply is observed at 80 ms, so round-trip time, or RTT, is 80 ms. This includes the chosen request/reply measurement path; it is not automatically the one-way link delay. Throughput uses a separate observation: \(1{,}000{,}000\) bytes over 2 seconds gives \(500{,}000\) bytes per second. Multiply by 8 bits per byte to get \(4{,}000{,}000\) bits per second. A rate describes how much data arrives per unit time; a delay describes how long an event takes. The wrapper for a local link may change at a router while the application’s request continues toward the same destination.
guide.exercise: For response times 40,60,50 ms compute mean RTT. If 2,000 bytes arrive in0.5 seconds, calculate bytes/s and bits/s. Draw which header belongs to link, IP, transport and application in a hypothetical request.
guide.solution: Add the RTT measurements: \(40+60+50=150\) ms; divide by three to obtain mean RTT \(50\) ms. For throughput, \(2000/0.5=4000\) bytes/s, then \(4000\times8=32{,}000\) bits/s. A hypothetical packet drawing has an outer link header, then an IP header, then transport information, then application data. The exact headers depend on the selected protocols. These calculations count the stated payload bytes; they do not establish total wire traffic including headers or retransmissions.
guide.challenge: A capture sees three packets of a five-packet transfer. Explain two reasons other than network loss that packets might be absent, and distinguish packet count from complete application messages.
guide.challenge_solution: Capture start/end timing, capture filters and observation location can omit packets. Several packets may compose one message; retransmissions may repeat bytes. State the capture vantage point before inferring loss.

N01.concept: A network carries messages between systems. Layers separate responsibilities: an application message can travel inside a transport segment, an IP packet, and a link-layer frame. Encapsulation adds headers used by each layer. The receiving system interprets and removes those wrappers in reverse order. A packet capture reveals observations at a particular point, not every event everywhere.
N01.mechanism: Latency measures delay; bandwidth measures a transfer rate. Throughput is the rate actually achieved under protocol and workload constraints. Packet loss, queueing, and repeated round trips can matter as much as link speed. Capture only your authorised lab traffic and identify the interface, time range, and capture filters in your notes.
N01.example: Fetch a page from your own local test server while capturing its traffic. Identify the link, network, transport, and application information visible in the capture. Compare a tiny request with a larger response. Estimate transfer time from size and rate, then identify the additional delays that the estimate omitted.
N01.pitfall: An encrypted payload can still reveal metadata such as endpoint addresses, timing, and sizes.

check.question: What does bandwidth measure?
choices: The delay of one packet by definition
A potential data-transfer rate
Whether a connection is authenticated
check.explanation: Bandwidth concerns rate. Latency concerns delay, and neither alone establishes security.

guide.bridge: From M01, convert one byte into eight binary digits and recall that six independent bits have 64 patterns. From N01, distinguish the next local hop from the final destination. All example addresses are reserved documentation examples; this is a paper exercise, not a request to change network settings.
guide.teaching:
Read an IPv4 address as four eight-bit groups written in decimal, each from 0 to 255. Thus 192.0.2.10 is a 32-bit value, not four unrelated labels. A prefix fixes some leading bits. In 192.0.2.0/24, the slash number says the first 24 bits identify the prefix, leaving eight variable bits. Those last bits span .0 through .255, giving 256 total addresses.

A mask writes the fixed positions as 1 and the remaining positions as 0. For /24 it is 255.255.255.0. A bitwise AND compares each pair of bits, keeping 1 only when both are 1; applying the mask keeps the prefix and clears the remaining positions. You do not have to memorise a subnet table if you can count the variable bits.

For /26, the first three bytes use 24 fixed bits and the last byte contributes two more. Its mask is 11000000 in that byte, or decimal 192. Six positions remain variable, giving 64 patterns. A /26 beginning at .0 spans .0–.63; one beginning at .64 spans .64–.127. Always check that the written starting address agrees with its prefix boundary.

An IP prefix identifies a network portion. In IPv4, /24 fixes 24 of 32 bits, leaving 8 bits for addresses in that prefix. Bitwise comparison with the mask determines whether two addresses share that prefix; similar-looking decimal numbers are not a reliable substitute.

A routing table selects a next hop, usually using the longest matching prefix. A default route /0 matches when no more specific route does. The next hop is a forwarding decision, not necessarily the final destination. NAT translates address/port mappings across a boundary; it is not a complete authorisation policy.

IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses and different operational conventions. Do not transfer IPv4 broadcast and NAT assumptions blindly. Addressing, routing, name resolution and firewall policy are separate layers: a valid route can exist while policy denies traffic, and a hostname can resolve to multiple addresses.

Header precision: IPv4’s IHL counts 32-bit words, so IHL=5 means 20 bytes. Its 16-bit total-length field allows at most 65535 bytes including header. IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses, a 40-byte base header and a 20-bit flow label; extension headers provide additional functions, and IPv6 routers do not fragment packets as IPv4 routers can. There is no IPv6 base-header checksum. The older video’s captions can flatten bit fields and addresses; use these explicit units. An autonomous system (AS) is a group operated under a routing policy. BGP advertises prefix reachability and path attributes between/within ASes. It does not certify a company’s geography or authorise an application request.

IPv6 writes 128 bits in eight groups of hexadecimal digits. For example, 2001:db8::1 expands to 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001; :: abbreviates one consecutive run of zero groups. The example is a documentation address, not a service to contact. A port is a transport-level number used to distinguish application conversations at an address; N04 explains it. A NAT device can rewrite address/port mappings, but rewriting where traffic appears to come from does not establish who is allowed to use an application.
guide.example:
Documentation network: 192.0.2.0/24
Mask: 255.255.255.0
192.0.2.10 and 192.0.2.200 share this /24.
192.0.3.10 does not.

Routes:
192.0.2.128/25 -> router B
192.0.2.0/24   -> router A
0.0.0.0/0     -> router D
Destination 192.0.2.200 selects B (longest prefix).
guide.explanation: The /25 divides the /24 into two groups of 128 addresses. .200 is in the upper group .128 through .255 and therefore matches both routes, but /25 is more specific. Host address allocation has additional rules; counting total bit patterns is not always the same as counting conventionally usable hosts.
guide.exercise: For 198.51.100.0/26, calculate total addresses and its numeric range. Given routes 198.51.100.0/24->A, 198.51.100.64/26->B, default->D, choose routes for .70, .10 and 203.0.113.5.
guide.solution: An IPv4 /26 leaves \(32-26=6\) variable bits, giving \(2^6=64\) total addresses. Starting at 198.51.100.0, they run through .63. Destination .70 falls inside .64–.127, so the /26 route to B wins over the matching /24 route to A. Destination .10 does not match that /26, but does match the /24, so choose A. 203.0.113.5 matches neither listed specific prefix, so choose the default D. These are total address counts; conventional IPv4 subnet reservations affect usable host counts separately.
guide.challenge: Explain why NAT does not prove a service is authorised, then compare address length for IPv4 and IPv6. For two routes /24 and /28 matching a destination, state which is selected under longest-prefix routing.
guide.challenge_solution: NAT is translation, not application identity/permission checking. IPv4 has 32 bits, IPv6 has 128. The /28 match is more specific, subject to the stated routing model and any additional policy rules.

N02.concept: IP addresses identify interfaces for packet delivery. A prefix specifies which leading bits define a network. Routing selects a next hop using destination prefixes; the most specific matching route normally wins. A subnet calculation is therefore a bit-boundary problem, not a guess based on how similar two dotted-decimal addresses look.
N02.mechanism: NAT translates addresses and often ports between address realms. It changes reachability and state tracking but is not a complete security policy. IPv6 has a larger address space and different conventions; do not transfer every IPv4 assumption to it. Routing between administrative networks also involves control-plane trust, including the routes exchanged through BGP.
N02.example: For 192.0.2.0/24, mark the first 24 bits as the network prefix. Divide it into two /25 prefixes and identify which half contains 192.0.2.130. Draw the route from a private lab host through a NAT gateway to a service, recording the source address seen on each side.
N02.pitfall: An address being private does not prove the host or traffic is trustworthy. Policy still needs explicit enforcement.

check.question: Which route normally wins when /16 and /24 entries both match a destination?
choices: The /16, because it covers more addresses
Whichever was mentioned first in a tutorial
The /24, because it has the longer matching prefix
check.explanation: Longest-prefix matching selects the more specific route, subject to the routing system's applicable rules.

guide.bridge: Builds on N02 addressing and N01 local-link delivery. Use synthetic records; do not alter shared wireless networks.
guide.teaching:
A device first needs to reach another device on its local link. Ethernet calls the unit it sends a frame, and uses a link-layer address, often called a MAC address, to choose the local recipient. MAC here means Media Access Control, not the cryptographic message-authentication code introduced later. This address and an IP address have different jobs. A frame can go to a router locally while its enclosed IP packet is still addressed to a distant server.

ARP stands for Address Resolution Protocol. It asks for the link address associated with a neighbouring IPv4 address: “who has the gateway’s IP address?” DHCP stands for Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol. It supplies a temporary address assignment, called a lease, and other configuration. Neither acronym means “verify this application’s identity”.

An IPv4 host needs a link-layer destination for a local next hop. ARP asks which local link address corresponds to an IPv4 address. For a remote IP destination, the host normally resolves the gateway's link address rather than the remote server's. ARP operates within the local link domain.

DHCP can provide an address lease and configuration such as subnet, router and DNS servers. The familiar discovery/offer/request/acknowledgement sequence is a negotiation, not proof that the configuration is trustworthy. DHCP and ARP do not by themselves establish application-server identity.

Wireless adds an association and link-protection layer. An SSID is a name, not a cryptographic proof of a trusted access point. Link encryption protects a particular segment under its assumptions; HTTPS still provides a separate end-to-end server-authentication boundary. Explain which party a control authenticates before concluding that a whole connection is safe.

For a new DHCP allocation, Discover, Offer, Request and ACK form one exchange with a matching transaction identifier. Renewing or restarting configuration is a separate case. Options can supply a netmask, router and DNS servers. Off-link traffic normally uses a gateway; same-subnet delivery need not pass through that router. IPv6 uses Neighbor Discovery rather than ARP and does not use IPv4 broadcast. A link address, an IP configuration lease and a trusted server identity answer different questions.

Translate the first-allocation DHCP sequence into a conversation. Discover asks for available configuration service. Offer proposes an address and options. Request identifies the offer the client is asking to use. ACK acknowledges the lease and configuration. A matching transaction identifier helps associate the replies with the exchange; it is not a cryptographic proof that the sender is trustworthy. An SSID is the advertised Wi-Fi network name. Recognising that name is different from verifying which access point you joined.
guide.example:
Host: 192.0.2.10/24, gateway 192.0.2.1
Target: 203.0.113.8 (remote)
1. Route chooses gateway 192.0.2.1.
2. ARP: who has 192.0.2.1?
3. Local response: gateway link address G.
4. Frame destination G; IP destination remains203.0.113.8.

DHCP teaching order: Discover -> Offer -> Request -> ACK
guide.explanation: The local frame goes to the router, while IP forwarding continues toward the remote destination. Seeing a gateway link address in a capture does not mean the gateway is the final application server. A rogue configuration source can influence routing or DNS without making an HTTPS certificate valid.
guide.exercise: For the host above, compare destinations192.0.2.20 and203.0.113.8. State whose link address is needed for each under the simple directly-connected/default-route model. Label the four DHCP messages and the configuration they aim to supply.
guide.solution: For 192.0.2.20, the /24 prefix matches the host’s own connected network; the frame needs .20’s link address. For 203.0.113.8, the simple route goes through gateway 192.0.2.1; ARP therefore asks for the gateway’s link address, not the remote server’s. The IP destination remains the remote server. DHCP Discover seeks a configuration offer; Offer proposes it; Request asks to use the selected offer; ACK confirms the lease/configuration. Options can include the address mask, gateway and DNS servers. This is the new-allocation teaching exchange, not every renewal sequence, and it does not authenticate every later application service.
guide.challenge: A cafe advertises an SSID matching your home network name. Explain why the name alone establishes no trust, and distinguish wireless link encryption, DNS resolution and HTTPS authentication.
guide.challenge_solution: The SSID is a selectable label. Link encryption concerns local radio traffic, DNS supplies name/address information, and HTTPS certificate validation authenticates the requested server name under the browser's trust model. None can be replaced by merely recognising a network name.

N03.concept: Ethernet frames deliver data on a local link using link-layer addresses. ARP resolves an IPv4 neighbour's address to a link-layer address. DHCP supplies configuration such as an address, gateway, and DNS server. These protocols solve different problems even when they appear together during a machine's network startup.
N03.mechanism: Local-link proximity is a trust concern. Traditional ARP does not authenticate every claimed mapping, so a neighbour's assertion is not equivalent to verified identity. Wireless access adds association, radio exposure, and link-security configuration. Protected Wi-Fi encrypts the link under its protocol and configuration; it does not replace end-to-end application security.
N03.example: Inside an isolated lab, record the interface address, assigned IP prefix, default route, and DNS configuration. Draw how a host learns a destination neighbour's link address versus how it learns a remote route. Use a saved capture to distinguish a DHCP configuration exchange from an ARP request without generating traffic on someone else's network.
N03.pitfall: A MAC address is not a durable proof of a person's or device's identity. It can be changed or represented by software.

check.question: Which protocol resolves an IPv4 neighbour to a link-layer address?
choices: ARP
HTTP
TLS
check.explanation: ARP handles this local-link mapping. HTTP is an application protocol and TLS protects a transport channel.

guide.bridge: From P04, distinguish text from UTF-8 bytes and run a saved Python file. From L01, open two terminal windows in the same practice folder. From N03, distinguish a local link from the application conversation. 127.0.0.1 is the loopback address: this exercise connects only within your own computer.
guide.teaching:
Think of TCP as an ordered stream of bytes, like numbered pieces of a continuous ribbon. It does not label where your application’s first message ends and its next begins. If you send hello followed by a newline, a receiver might get he and then llo plus the newline, or all of it at once. Framing is the rule for recognising a complete message. Our first rule is simple: a line ends at the newline byte and cannot exceed 100 bytes including that newline.

A socket is the OS interface a program uses for communication. For this exercise, the server waits for a connection and the client starts it. A port number chooses the listening endpoint on that computer; it is not a user identity. Python writes byte strings with a b prefix: b"hello\n" contains bytes including a final newline. A normal string can be converted with .encode("utf-8"); the receiving application needs an agreed decoding rule to turn bytes back into text.

TCP provides an ordered byte stream between endpoints. A send call does not create an application message boundary, and recv may return fewer bytes than requested. A protocol must define framing, such as a fixed length, delimiter or length prefix, and handle closure and limits.

UDP carries individual datagrams but does not supply TCP's retransmission and ordering behaviour. An application may add those features if needed. Ports distinguish transport endpoints; they do not prove the identity of a user or the safety of an application.

For a first socket exercise, use a local-only server, small bounded input and an explicit terminator. Run the server in one terminal and the client in another. If a port is already used, choose another unused local port in both files. A production protocol needs timeouts, authentication, resource limits and more robust error handling than this demonstration.

A TCP client normally starts CLOSED, actively sends SYN and enters SYN-SENT; the server listens and replies SYN-ACK. With initial sequence numbers x and y, the third message acknowledges y+1 and the server’s SYN-ACK acknowledges x+1. SYN consumes one sequence number. Closing is separate in each direction: A sends FIN, B acknowledges it, B later sends its own FIN and A acknowledges that. ACK and FIN can be combined, but are not required to be; the active closer normally waits in TIME-WAIT before CLOSED. Acknowledging received bytes is distinct from the application consuming them. The advertised receive window and the congestion window impose different limits on sending.

A socket is a program’s endpoint for communication. A TCP connection is distinguished by local IP, local port, remote IP and remote port within TCP. A TCP port and a UDP port with the same number are separate endpoints. The video’s destination-port-only UDP example assumes one local address and an unconnected socket; connected UDP and binding/reuse rules can also select by local/remote addresses. A port does not authenticate a user.

ACK means a positive acknowledgement; NAK is a negative acknowledgement in the teaching model. For a lost-ACK trace, send packet 1, deliver packet 1 once, then lose ACK 1. The sender times out and retransmits packet 1. The receiver recognises the duplicate, does not deliver it again, and sends ACK 1 again. A premature timer can produce the same retransmission even when the original acknowledgement was merely delayed. Model assumptions about corruption detection, packet lifetime and sequence-number wrap-around are part of the correctness claim. TCP numbers bytes: receiving bytes 100 through 119 contiguously leads to ACK 120, the next byte expected. This is different from the toy Go-Back-N packet-number convention. An acknowledgement from TCP does not prove the application committed a purchase or other side effect.

UDP’s checksum includes its header/data and an IP pseudo-header and can miss some corruption. It is not a cryptographic check. IPv4 permits an absent UDP checksum represented by zero; IPv6 normally requires one, with narrowly specified exceptions. UDP has no inherent congestion control, so protocols using it must supply appropriate behaviour. HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP; QUIC supplies transport functions beyond UDP itself. A congested network can still drop UDP datagrams.

For the socket video, socket() creates an endpoint, not a connection. A normal TCP client calls connect(); the server binds and listens, then accept() returns a separate connected socket. Data goes through that connected socket. A TCP send can write fewer bytes than requested and recv can return a partial message or several messages combined. Define framing, such as a bounded length prefix, and loop until that frame is complete; sendall handles sending the supplied bytes but does not prove the peer processed them. Python 3 sockets exchange bytes: text.encode("utf-8") produces bytes and received_bytes.decode("utf-8") interprets them. Empty bytes from TCP recv indicate end of stream; a zero-length UDP datagram has a different meaning. Keep any practice on an explicitly local disposable fixture, add timeouts and size limits, and close sockets reliably. No external connection is required for the native paper trace.

The revised example puts time and size limits on both sides. settimeout makes a stalled operation fail instead of waiting forever. b"" is an empty byte string; data += part appends the newly received bytes. recv(100-len(data)) asks for no more than the remaining capacity, but may return fewer bytes. An empty result means TCP ended, not “try again until data appears”. sendall sends the supplied bytes or raises an error; it still does not prove that the other application completed a requested action.
guide.example:
# server.py — run this file first in terminal 1
import socket
with socket.socket() as server:
    server.settimeout(60)  # time allowed to start the client
    server.bind(("127.0.0.1", 8765))
    server.listen(1)
    conn, address = server.accept()
    with conn:
        conn.settimeout(3)
        data = b""
        while b"\n" not in data and len(data) < 100:
            part = conn.recv(100 - len(data))
            if not part:
                break
            data += part
        reply = b"OK\n" if data == b"hello\n" else b"NO\n"
        conn.sendall(reply)

# client.py — save separately; run in terminal 2
import socket
with socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1", 8765), timeout=3) as client:
    client.sendall(b"hello\n")
    reply = b""
    while b"\n" not in reply and len(reply) < 100:
        part = client.recv(100 - len(reply))
        if not part:
            break
        reply += part
    if not reply.endswith(b"\n"):
        raise ValueError("Incomplete response line")
    print(reply)
# Expected client output: b'OK\n'; server exits after this one request.
guide.explanation: Copy the first program into server.py and the second into a separate client.py. Their matching address/port identifies this local conversation. The server accepts one connection, reads a bounded request and sends a bounded response. The client also accumulates the response until a newline; it does not assume a single recv gives the whole message. This tiny protocol accepts only exactly hello plus newline, rejects other accumulated data, and closes after one request. It is not a reusable multi-message server. A timeout is reported as an error; this demonstration does not pretend to recover a stalled transaction.
guide.exercise: Save the two separate files in your practice folder. In terminal 1 run python3 server.py using the Python command for your setup; within a minute, run python3 client.py in terminal 2. If your command is python, use it for both. If the port is already occupied, choose another unused local port in both files. Record the reply. Change the client payload to b"bye\n", restart the server and run the client again. Then trace on paper the two reads b"he" and b"llo\n" and show how data grows. A split into two actual send calls does not force the network to create two recv results; the paper trace makes that case reproducible.
guide.solution: The accepted response is OK and the changed message gives NO. Accumulated data becomes b"he", then b"hello\n". TCP can split or coalesce writes, so a single recv equality check is not a framing design.
guide.challenge: Design a length-prefixed teaching protocol with a maximum 16-byte payload. State what happens for announced lengths 0,5,17 and a five-byte payload delivered in two reads. Compare with a UDP datagram of length 5.
guide.challenge_solution: Explicitly choose whether zero is allowed, accept5, reject17 before allocation, and loop until all 5 bytes arrive or EOF/timeout occurs. A UDP receive observes datagram boundaries subject to buffer/truncation rules, but delivery/order is not guaranteed by UDP.

N04.concept: TCP provides an ordered byte stream with retransmission and congestion control. It does not preserve application message boundaries. UDP sends datagrams without TCP's delivery and ordering guarantees. An application chooses a protocol according to the behaviour it needs and implements any additional reliability, framing, or security itself.
N04.mechanism: A socket is an operating-system interface for network communication. TCP applications must define framing: a length, delimiter, or established message grammar tells the receiver when a message is complete. A single send call need not correspond to a single receive call. Timeouts and partial reads are ordinary conditions to handle, not impossible edge cases.
N04.example: Build a loopback-only client and server that exchange length-prefixed harmless messages. Deliberately split a message across writes and combine two messages in another write. The receiver should reconstruct both correctly. Compare this with a UDP example and document what happens when a datagram is absent rather than assuming arrival.
N04.pitfall: TCP reliability does not authenticate the peer or encrypt the stream. Those are separate properties.

check.question: A TCP receive call returns half your message. What should a correct framed protocol do?
choices: Assume the remaining bytes cannot exist
Keep reading until the defined message length is available or an error occurs
Treat every receive result as one complete message
check.explanation: TCP exposes a byte stream. The application's framing rule determines message completeness.

guide.bridge: Builds on N04 transport and N02 routing. Resolve only documentation names on paper; no mail sending is required.
guide.teaching:
A person remembers a service name such as www.example; the network needs an address. DNS is the distributed system used to answer questions about names. A resolver is the service your client asks to find the answer. An authoritative server supplies the records for a particular zone, meaning a managed part of the name hierarchy. Think of a directory with responsibility delegated to smaller directories, not one address book stored on one machine.

A cache keeps an answer so it need not be fetched repeatedly. TTL means time to live, measured here in seconds. An answer cached with TTL 300 can remain usable for roughly five minutes under the stated caching rules. Updating the authoritative data does not instantly replace every cached copy.

DNS maps names to typed records through a hierarchy and caches. A client typically asks a recursive resolver, which may query authoritative servers or use cached data. TTL limits cache lifetime under the protocol; it is not a promise that the service address never changes.

A records carry IPv4 addresses, AAAA IPv6, CNAME aliases and MX mail routing information. Resolution supplies data about a name; it does not by itself authenticate an HTTPS application. DNSSEC can authenticate signed DNS data under its trust chain, but it is distinct from encrypting the transport to a resolver.

Email combines routing, transfer and message interpretation. SPF, DKIM and DMARC address particular sending-domain/authentication policies; they do not prove every message claim is true or safe to act on. A displayed friendly sender name is not a verified identity. Evaluate the actual domain, authentication results, requested action and independent context.

DNS record types answer different questions: A gives an IPv4 address, AAAA gives an IPv6 address, and MX names a mail exchanger whose address is resolved separately. A recursive resolver commonly answers the client and makes iterative upstream queries; authoritative root/TLD servers do not normally recurse for the client. Cached TTLs reduce repeated work but make changes non-instantaneous. For email, distinguish SMTP server relay (port 25) from client submission (commonly 587, or 465 with implicit TLS) and IMAP retrieval. The SMTP envelope and visible From/To headers can differ. Modern message formats, MIME and negotiated extensions go beyond the legacy ASCII-only teaching model; TLS protection also needs an explicit endpoint and validation policy.

Read a record as columns: name, TTL, class, type, value. In the example, IN denotes the Internet class; A asks for IPv4 data. A CNAME value is another name to resolve, while MX names a mail server and includes a preference number. A trailing dot writes a complete DNS name. None of these values is an instruction to contact a real host in this exercise.

For later security readings: a digital signature is a checkable cryptographic claim about data made using a signing key; S04 explains its mathematics and trust assumptions. DNSSEC adds such validation to signed DNS data under a chain of trust. It does not make an address safe to visit. For mail, SPF concerns permitted sending infrastructure, DKIM signs selected message content under a domain, and DMARC connects domain-alignment checks and published handling policy. Those are domain-level signals, not guarantees that a person’s request is honest. You need not configure them to complete this paper lookup.
guide.example:
Invented zone:
notes.example. 300 IN A 192.0.2.10
www.example.   300 IN CNAME notes.example.
example.       300 IN MX 10 mail.example.
mail.example.  300 IN A 192.0.2.20

At t=0 resolver caches notes.example with TTL300.
At t=120 remaining lifetime is about180 seconds.
guide.explanation: The alias points to another DNS name rather than directly to an address. The MX preference10 is a routing priority value, not a port. A cached result can remain visible until expiry even after an authoritative update. The .example names are reserved teaching data.
guide.exercise: Using the records above, trace lookup of www.example through its alias to an IPv4 address. Calculate remaining TTL at t=250. Explain why successful lookup does not establish that an email claiming to be from support is legitimate.
guide.solution: The www.example record is a CNAME pointing to notes.example. Resolve that name’s A record to obtain 192.0.2.10. At t=250, subtract 250 from the original 300-second TTL: approximately 50 seconds remain in this simplified model. The number 10 in the MX record is mail preference, not a transport port. Successful resolution says which address the records returned; it does not verify a displayed human sender, prove the mail server is uncompromised or authorise disclosure of a password.
guide.challenge: Classify the purpose of AAAA, MX and CNAME. A message passes domain authentication but asks you to reveal a password. Explain what the authentication result does and does not establish, without sending or opening any message attachment.
guide.challenge_solution: AAAA supplies IPv6 data; MX mail routing; CNAME an alias. Domain authentication can support a domain-level provenance/policy claim; it does not establish benign content, uncompromised sender intent or authorisation to request secrets.

N05.concept: DNS maps names to records, such as address records used to locate a service. Resolvers may cache answers according to their time-to-live. Email delivery uses DNS records to locate mail servers and additional mechanisms to express sender-domain policies. A familiar-looking name is not the same thing as verified control of a service.
N05.mechanism: Separate the question 'Which address was returned?' from 'Why should I trust this answer or peer?' DNSSEC can authenticate signed DNS data through a chain of trust, but it does not encrypt ordinary DNS queries or make the destination application trustworthy. Email authentication mechanisms also have specific scopes; no single record guarantees that a message is harmless.
N05.example: Trace a domain lookup using the course's examples and mark stub resolver, recursive resolver, authoritative server, and cache. Inspect a saved DNS response and identify the record type and TTL. Then draw mail delivery from sender to recipient, marking where name resolution and sender-policy checks occur.
N05.pitfall: A correct DNS answer can point to a compromised server. Name-resolution integrity and application security are separate checks.

check.question: What property does DNSSEC primarily add to signed DNS data?
choices: Encryption of all DNS query contents
A guarantee that the website has no vulnerabilities
Origin authentication and integrity through a validation chain
check.explanation: DNSSEC validates signed DNS data. It neither encrypts ordinary DNS traffic nor audits the destination service.

guide.bridge: Builds on N05 names and N04 byte streams. Inspect the supplied HTTP transcript before using developer tools.
guide.teaching:
Imagine clicking “show my notes”. The browser sends a request describing what it wants; the server sends a response with a result. In the supplied transcript, GET is the method, /notes is the target path and Host identifies the requested host. Header lines carry named metadata in name: value form. A blank line separates headers from any message body. The JSON {"notes":[]} is response content: an empty list of notes, not a command for the browser to execute.

Stateless means HTTP itself does not automatically remember that two separate requests belong to one continuing user interaction. An application can add a session, meaning stored context for that interaction. A cookie is name/value data a browser may send on later eligible requests. Here session=DEMO_ONLY is an invented session credential. The application must validate it; a cookie being present does not prove the sender is authorised.

HTTP separates a request method and target from headers and optional content. A response carries a status, headers and optional content. Header names and their semantics matter: a 200 response indicates an application response, not a security approval.

Cookies connect later requests with stored state. The server sets a cookie, and the browser decides when to send it under domain, path, Secure, SameSite and other rules. HttpOnly restricts script access to a cookie; it does not stop the browser from sending it with eligible requests. A session identifier should be treated as a credential.

Caches reuse responses under defined policy. Shared caches and private browser caches have different users and trust boundaries. A proxy can terminate one connection and make another, so the application must know which forwarding metadata it can trust. Do not assume a user-supplied forwarded header is authoritative just because it names an IP address.

Client and server describe roles in an exchange. A reverse proxy can receive a browser request as a server and make an upstream request as a client; a service can perform both roles. Hostnames can resolve to changing or multiple server addresses, and a well-known port is a convention rather than proof of service identity.

The video’s readable request lines illustrate HTTP/1.1. HTTP/2 carries messages using binary frames over TCP, and HTTP/3 maps HTTP semantics onto QUIC over UDP. The text transcript above is a teaching representation rather than the HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 wire format. Reusing a connection avoids repeated setup; first connections, TLS, response sizes, parallel requests and congestion still affect total latency. Ordinary TCP supplies neither encryption nor peer authentication. HTTPS adds a configured secure transport; certificate validation and application authorisation remain different checks.

HTTP being stateless does not forbid a server-side session. A cookie is name/value data, not necessarily a number. Set-Cookie delivers it to a browser; a later Cookie request header can carry it back when browser rules permit. The numeric shopping example is illustrative; do not assume every cookie identifies an authenticated person or that every server records a complete history. HttpOnly restricts script access but does not make all requests trustworthy.

Cache-Control: no-cache normally permits storage but requires successful validation before reuse; no-store forbids storage by compliant caches. private prevents shared-cache storage, while public can explicitly allow shared caching. Validators describe a representation: reuse an ETag in If-None-Match, or the server’s Last-Modified timestamp in If-Modified-Since, rather than substituting your local download time. For an applicable cached GET, 304 carries no replacement content and tells the cache to reuse/update its stored response metadata; a changed successful GET normally returns 200 with content. Cache keys and Vary matter, and a cache hit is not automatically safe for personalised data.

Trace the two directions separately. Cookie travels from browser to server on a request. Set-Cookie travels from server to browser on a response and asks the browser to store or update a cookie according to its rules. Status 200 reports a successful response; it does not certify the permission check. Content-Type names the representation format. A cache is a stored response for possible reuse; private and no-store control different aspects of that reuse. For the exercise, identify these lines before reading the more detailed HTTP-version and cache-validation notes above.
guide.example:
GET /notes HTTP/1.1
Host: notes.example
Cookie: session=DEMO_ONLY

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Cache-Control: private, no-store
Set-Cookie: session=NEW_DEMO; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax

{"notes":[]}

These are fictional credentials; never paste a real cookie into notes.
guide.explanation: The browser sends a Cookie header in the request; the server sends Set-Cookie in the response. Secure restricts the cookie to secure transport in normal browser handling. no-store tells compliant caches not to store the response, while private excludes shared-cache storage when caching would otherwise be permitted. These flags address different mechanisms.
guide.exercise: Annotate method, path, host, request credential, status, representation type and storage policy in the transcript. Explain what changes when the cookie is absent and why the answer depends on application policy rather than HTTP alone.
guide.solution: The first line supplies method GET and path /notes. Host supplies notes.example. Cookie carries the invented session value used as a credential in this application. The response line reports status 200; Content-Type identifies JSON, and Cache-Control says private, no-store. Set-Cookie requests a new cookie with its listed attributes. If the request has no session cookie, the application might reject it, redirect to sign-in or provide a deliberately public response: HTTP alone does not choose. For protected notes, its authorisation policy must prevent an unauthenticated caller from receiving private content.
guide.challenge: A response contains private user notes and Cache-Control: public,max-age=600. Explain the risk in a shared cache, propose a safer policy and give one verification case involving two invented users.
guide.challenge_solution: Public storage can reuse a private representation across users if cache keys/policy permit it. Use a deliberate private/no-store policy for sensitive content and verify that user B never receives user A's response. Cookie flags alone do not fix shared response caching.

N06.concept: HTTP describes requests and responses. A request has a method, target, headers, and sometimes a body; a response has a status, headers, and possibly a body. HTTP is stateless in its basic request-response model. Cookies and server-side sessions let applications associate requests with continuing state.
N06.mechanism: Proxies forward messages and caches reuse responses according to rules. This creates several possible interpretations of a request, so understand the path before analysing behaviour. Cookie attributes influence when browsers send cookies and which scripts can access them. HTTPS protects the channel, but the application must still validate input and authorise actions.
N06.example: Use a local test application to record a GET and a form POST. Mark each method, path, status, content type, and cookie. Repeat after signing out and observe which state changes. Add a diagram showing browser, proxy if present, and server, so a later security finding can identify where a decision was made.
N06.pitfall: A successful status code means the server reported success for that request; it does not prove the action was authorised correctly.

check.question: Why do many applications use a session cookie?
choices: To associate separate HTTP requests with server-recognised state
Because TCP requires passwords in every packet
To make browser-side input validation sufficient
check.explanation: A session identifier links otherwise separate requests to application state. Its protection and authorisation checks remain essential.

guide.bridge: You have used Python variables and functions (P02/P03) and traced HTTP requests (N06). Here the browser runs JavaScript instead of Python. Save the example as greet.html using a plain-text editor, then open that file in your browser. No server or account is needed.
guide.teaching:
HTML describes document structure. The DOM is the browser's live object model of that document. JavaScript reads events and updates nodes. A form is a data-entry structure; its client-side validation improves interaction but cannot enforce server-side trust rules.

Text and markup are different. Assigning textContent inserts literal text, while interpreting a value as HTML asks the browser to parse markup. Use text insertion for untrusted plain text. Later XSS lessons explain why context-specific handling matters when data enters executable or markup contexts.

A web origin is normally scheme, host and port. Paths do not create separate origins. https://notes.example/a and /b share an origin, while changing scheme, host or effective port can change it. Locally opened file URLs have special browser rules, so use the assigned hosted training environment for cross-origin security labs rather than assuming file behaviour matches HTTPS.

An id identifies a DOM element for selectors; a form field’s name identifies its submitted key. They need not match. The form action chooses the destination, and method chooses how fields are submitted; GET normally places the encoded fields in the URL query. Query values are untrusted input, and URL encoding is not authentication or encryption. A submit-button click or Enter can trigger form submission; preventDefault on a submit listener can deliberately keep the interaction local. A click listener on a standalone button is another event.

Keep an explicit visible label associated with an input. Placeholder text disappears as someone types and is not a replacement for that label. The provided script is after its referenced nodes; otherwise use an appropriate loading strategy before querying them. No match from querySelector returns null, so a misspelled selector cannot be treated as an element. Both value and textContent here handle literal text, including angle brackets. Server-side checks remain required even when the local interaction looks correct.

Read the script from outside in. document is the current page; querySelector("#name") finds the element whose id is name. The dot accesses a property or method, just as in Python objects. const declares a variable that will not be reassigned here. addEventListener registers a function to run later when a click happens. The () => { ... } expression is that function; braces surround its body and semicolons separate statements. The script registers the action when the page loads; it reads the input only when the button is clicked.
guide.explanation: The event listener runs after a click. value is text from the input; textContent displays it literally. Typing Fav should show the angle brackets and letters rather than a bold element. This is a harmless way to observe parsing boundaries without running an attack payload.
guide.exercise: Save greet.html and run it. Enter Fav and then the literal text Fav. Record the output and inspect the result node in browser developer tools. Compare origins https://a.example/x, https://a.example/y and https://b.example/x.
guide.solution: The two a.example URLs share an origin. b.example differs. The result contains literal text and does not gain a nested b element when textContent is used.
guide.challenge: Add a Reset button that clears both input and output. Explain why a required input attribute cannot replace a server-side rule that a user may edit only their own record.

B01.concept: HTML defines document structure, CSS controls presentation, and JavaScript can change behaviour. The DOM is the browser's object representation of a document. Browser scripts can read or modify permitted parts of that representation, respond to events, and make network requests. Treat user-supplied text as data rather than executable markup.
B01.mechanism: An origin consists of scheme, host, and port. Browser security rules use this boundary when deciding which scripts may access which resources. A site, an origin, and a full URL are different concepts. Form validation in the browser improves usability, but a client can send a request without running that validation, so the server must enforce its own requirements.
B01.example: Create a local page with a form and a text-only preview. Use textContent to show the submitted value. Enter text that resembles an HTML tag and confirm it remains visible text. Compare two local URLs with different ports and explain why they have different origins even though their hostnames match.
B01.pitfall: Hiding a button or disabling a field in JavaScript does not prevent a user from constructing the corresponding request.

check.question: Which components define a web origin?
choices: Only the page's visible title
Scheme, host, and port
The path and query string alone
check.explanation: The origin tuple excludes the path and query. Different ports or schemes can create different origins on the same host.

guide.bridge: Builds on P04 structured data and M02 invariants. Python includes sqlite3, so this fixture requires no database account.
guide.teaching:
Imagine a spreadsheet with columns id, owner and body. In this database each horizontal record is a row and each named property is a column. A schema declares the allowed structure. INTEGER means a whole number; TEXT means character data. PRIMARY KEY makes id identify a row uniquely. SELECT body chooses the output column; FROM notes names the table; WHERE owner=? keeps only matching rows. The ? is a value placeholder supplied separately, and fetchall returns a Python list of result tuples. The comma in ("a",) makes a one-item tuple.

A relational table organises rows under named columns. A primary key identifies a row; a foreign key can express a relationship. A query selects data according to a predicate. A schema describes permitted structure, while application rules add meaning such as ownership.

Parameterised queries keep values separate from SQL syntax. Placeholders represent data, not table names or arbitrary SQL fragments. Build the fixed query structure in code and bind user-controlled values through the database API. Validation and parameterisation solve related but different problems.

A transaction groups changes into a consistent unit. Isolation affects what concurrent transactions can observe, and constraints enforce invariants even if a client makes a mistake. A check-then-update sequence can race unless the whole invariant is protected. A successful single-user query does not demonstrate concurrent correctness.

A relational model is not defined simply by drawing arrows: constraints specify which rows may exist. A primary key may contain multiple columns, and a foreign key must be declared and enforced to reject orphan references. SQLite connections should explicitly enable PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON when relying on those constraints. NULL handling and NOT NULL requirements need deliberate policy. A join can multiply rows when multiple matches exist; an inner join excludes unmatched rows. SQL result order is unspecified without ORDER BY, and LIMIT alone does not choose the highest-rated rows.

For the native stock example, distinguish lost update from negative stock. If both clients read 1, compute a new value 0 and each writes 0, the final value is nonnegative but two sales consumed one item. If each later issues quantity=quantity-1 without a predicate, the value can become -1. A conditional single-row update with quantity>=1 plus an affected-row check prevents that row’s oversell under the chosen database contract. Wrapping arbitrary statements in BEGIN/COMMIT alone is not a universal concurrency repair. SQLite permits one writer at a time and can return SQLITE_BUSY; handle contention and transaction state deliberately. The paper schedule is reasoning evidence, not a performed concurrency test.
guide.example:
import sqlite3
con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
con.execute("CREATE TABLE notes(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, owner TEXT, body TEXT)")
con.executemany("INSERT INTO notes VALUES(?,?,?)", [(1,"a","alpha"),(2,"b","beta")])
rows = con.execute("SELECT body FROM notes WHERE owner=?", ("a",)).fetchall()
print(rows)
# [('alpha',)]
# The tuple comma in ("a",) is intentional.
guide.explanation: The query text is fixed while the owner value is bound separately. Fetching owner a returns only alpha in this dataset. In a real app, owner must come from the authenticated identity, not a request parameter that a caller can change. Parameterisation alone does not establish ownership.
guide.exercise: Run the in-memory fixture. Query owner b and owner missing. Add a third row owned by a and predict the result set. Explain the roles of a primary key and the ownership predicate.
guide.solution: Replace the final query value with ("b",) to get [("beta",)]; ("missing",) gives []. Insert a new row with con.execute("INSERT INTO notes VALUES(?,?,?)", (3, "a", "gamma")), then query a again: the result contains ("alpha",) and ("gamma",) in unspecified order. Add ORDER BY id after the WHERE clause if that order matters. The primary key rejects a second id 1; the WHERE condition selects ownership in this fixture. In a real API the owner value must come from verified identity.
guide.challenge: Paper stock model: quantity starts at 1. Client A reads 1, client B reads 1, and each records a sale and writes its precomputed value 0. Explain why this oversells despite never storing -1. Then consider two unconditional quantity=quantity-1 updates. Write a single conditional update and state the success check that should gate each sale. No concurrent runtime test is required.
guide.challenge_solution: Lost-update trace: A reads 1; B reads 1; A writes 0 and records a sale; B writes 0 and records another sale. Two sales consumed one item even though stored quantity is 0. With two unconditional decrements the successive values can instead be 0 and -1. A conditional statement is UPDATE stock SET quantity=quantity-1 WHERE id=? AND quantity>=1. Exactly one affected row means that decrement succeeded; zero means no eligible stock row, so do not record the sale. The sale record and stock change must share a deliberate transaction design. Isolation, error handling and retries remain database-specific; this paper trace does not verify a production implementation.

B02.concept: A relational database stores rows in tables with declared columns and constraints. A primary key identifies a row; a foreign key relates it to another table. SQL expresses queries and updates. A join combines related rows according to an explicit relationship, so a mistaken join can multiply results or reveal unrelated records.
B02.mechanism: A transaction groups operations into one logical unit. Atomicity means they commit together or not at all. Isolation controls what concurrent transactions may observe; different isolation levels provide different guarantees. Constraints such as unique keys and valid relationships can protect invariants closer to the data rather than relying on every caller to remember a rule.
B02.example: Create synthetic users and notes tables. Give each note an owner_id referencing a user. Join notes with owners and verify the row count. In a transaction, transfer a fixed quantity between two rows; introduce a failure between the updates and check rollback. Write down which invariant the transaction protects.
B02.pitfall: An application checking uniqueness before insertion can still race. A database uniqueness constraint enforces the rule at the storage boundary.

check.question: What does transaction atomicity promise?
choices: Every query runs instantly
Any logged-in user can read every row
All operations in the transaction commit together or none do
check.explanation: Atomicity concerns the all-or-nothing unit of change. It does not by itself establish performance or authorisation.

guide.bridge: Builds on B02 ownership and N06 requests. The API flow below is an offline design fixture; it does not require deploying a server.
guide.teaching:
Think of an API as an agreed way to ask a program for something. A request contains an operation and inputs; the response says what happened. For GET /api/notes/1, GET is the method and /api/notes/1 is the path. A route selects the handler function for that method/path. A contract documents accepted inputs and outputs. In this example the session identifies A, the path identifies note 1, and the server must check that A owns note 1 before returning it.

An API is a contract for requests, responses and errors. A server parses the request, authenticates the caller, validates input, authorises the operation and performs a state change. These are separate decisions: valid JSON does not imply a valid business operation.

A session associates requests with an authenticated identity. Keep the server-side identity separate from user-supplied owner fields. If an API accepts note_id=2, it must still verify that the authenticated caller may access note2. Returning a consistent error can avoid unnecessary disclosure, but hiding identifiers is not a substitute for the check.

Structured data needs a schema and size limits. Reject unexpected types and decide how unknown fields are handled. Error responses should be useful without exposing secrets or stack traces. For state changes, specify what happens if a client retries after losing the response; advanced distributed-systems lessons revisit this ambiguity.

Flask routes connect a URL/method pattern to a Python view function. A decorator registers that association; a function name is not itself the URL. request.args accesses query values, request.form parsed form fields, and JSON parsing is a distinct operation with its own type/size checks. render_template combines a template with supplied data; HTML escaping is context-specific and does not turn arbitrary data into trusted JavaScript, CSS or URLs. jsonify serialises supported values as JSON; JSON syntax does not establish business meaning or caller permissions.

A session can outlive a TCP connection. Set-Cookie is a response header asking the browser to store cookie data; Cookie is a request header carrying eligible cookies under browser policy. Flask’s default session stores signed data on the client: the signature detects unauthorised modification under the secret key, but does not hide the data. Server-side session storage requires a separate design. Never put passwords or confidential data into a merely signed cookie. A stolen usable session can still grant authority, so expiry, revocation and the application’s object checks remain separate concerns. The development server is for local practice; it is not a production deployment plan.
guide.example:
Invented data: note1 owner=A; note2 owner=B
GET /api/notes/1, session identity A -> 200 {"id":1,"body":"demo"}
GET /api/notes/2, session identity A -> 404 or403 by documented policy
GET /api/notes/1, no session       -> 401 by this API's policy
POST /api/notes, identity A, body {"body":7} -> 400
POST /api/notes, identity A, body {"body":"hi","owner":"B"}
  -> reject unknown owner field; never transfer ownership from input
guide.explanation: The same target identifier produces different decisions based on the authenticated principal. This contract chooses400 for type/shape errors and rejects an owner field. Other APIs may use different documented status conventions, but the ownership invariant should remain the same.
guide.exercise: Write a decision table for every supplied request. Add valid creation {"body":"hi"} under A and an oversized body over your chosen100-character practice limit. State stored owner and expected response category.
guide.solution: Using this fixture policy: A reading note 1 gets 200 and its body; A reading B’s note 2 gets 404 (or a consistently documented 403); no session gets 401. Creation with numeric body 7 gets 400; a supplied owner field gets 400 under the reject-unknown-fields rule. Creation with only {"body":"hi"} stores owner A from the verified session and can return 201 with the new id. A body of 101 characters exceeds the chosen 100-character limit and gets 400 with a safe explanation. These status choices describe this invented API; the ownership and validation decisions are the security requirements.
guide.challenge: Design DELETE /api/notes/{id} for the same invented records. Include unauthenticated, owner, non-owner and nonexistent-object cases. Explain whether repeating a successful deletion should change another object.
guide.challenge_solution: Only the authorised owner can delete its object. Repeated deletion must not affect unrelated records. The API should document how missing objects are reported and consistently avoid ownership bypass; status-code choice alone is not the security guarantee.

B03.concept: A web server receives HTTP requests, routes them to application code, and returns responses. An API is a defined interface to application operations. JSON and XML are data formats, not permission systems. A session identifies continuing state, while object ownership determines whether a particular actor may perform a particular action.
B03.mechanism: Draw the full boundary: request bytes, parsed values, validated input, authenticated actor, authorised operation, database change, response. Each step answers a different question. Keep server secrets out of browser code. Return controlled errors rather than exposing stack traces or internal credentials. Use a development server only under the scope and deployment guidance of the exercise.
B03.example: Build a small local notes API with synthetic users. On each read or update, obtain the current actor from trusted session state and check the note's owner on the server. Reject an invalid note identifier cleanly. Test the same request as the owner and as another test user, and compare results.
B03.pitfall: A valid session does not grant access to every object's data. Authentication and object-level authorisation are separate steps.

check.question: Where must ownership be checked when updating a note?
choices: On the server handling the operation
Only in the browser's menu rendering
Only in the API's prose documentation
check.explanation: A caller can bypass the interface. The server must enforce the relationship between actor, object, and requested action.

guide.bridge: Builds on C06 operating-system boundaries and L03 reproducibility. Choose the linked platform setup appropriate to your computer; a container is not a replacement for every VM boundary.
guide.teaching:
A VM is like a separate practice computer running inside your computer. Its operating system is the guest; your physical computer is the host. The hypervisor is the software layer providing virtual hardware. RAM is working memory, virtual disk is saved storage, and a network interface connects the guest to selected networks. A container is closer to giving a program its own view of folders and processes while using the engine host’s operating-system kernel. These analogies explain the arrangement, not a promise of perfect containment.

A virtual machine runs a guest operating system behind a hypervisor boundary. A container usually shares its host kernel while isolating selected resources and namespaces. These different trust models matter when choosing where to run unfamiliar software. A container configured with excessive host access can undermine its intended boundary.

A snapshot records a recoverable state under the tool's rules. It is not automatically an independent backup and may include sensitive data. Keep a clean baseline, record network mode and define how to restore it before starting a lab. Disable unnecessary shared folders, credentials and exposed services.

A reproducible lab record states host/guest versions, allocated resources, image provenance, network configuration and expected observations. Verify isolation with harmless checks: an intentionally local training server should not listen on every interface. Do not infer total containment from one successful test. Where hardware cannot support the required platform, use the provider's designated training environment rather than improvising on a shared production device.

For Linux containers, namespaces separate views of resources, cgroups account for and limit selected resources, and capabilities/seccomp/security policy restrict selected operations. None alone proves containment. Containers share the engine host’s kernel; on Docker Desktop that engine commonly lives in a Linux VM. A Docker-daemon handle can grant substantial host authority even when the application runs as a non-root user. A VM normally has its own guest kernel; hosted and bare-metal hypervisors have different surrounding trust requirements. A language virtual machine is another abstraction again. Explicit shared folders, ports, clipboard/agent channels, credentials and external services remain boundaries to review. Restoring a VM snapshot does not undo writes already sent to those external resources.
guide.example:
Lab plan (paper fixture)
Host: your own computer
Guest: supported training Linux VM
Network: NAT or isolated mode chosen for the exercise
Shared folders: none initially
Credentials: invented lab-only values
Baseline: clean-setup snapshot
Recovery check: create marker.txt, restore baseline, confirm marker absent
Exposed app: loopback only unless the lab explicitly requires otherwise
guide.explanation: The marker test checks restoration behaviour without introducing hostile software. It does not prove that every disk or external volume is covered by the snapshot. Record which state is excluded. NAT connectivity is not an automatic assurance that all traffic or inbound access is forbidden.
guide.exercise: Produce the full lab plan above for your selected platform. If a supported VM is available, perform the harmless marker restore. Otherwise complete the paper plan and explicitly label the runtime restore check unperformed; do not mark it as verified.
guide.solution: Example paper plan: supported Linux guest from the training provider’s official image; record exact image version and download source; allocate RAM/disk within that platform’s documented requirements and your available capacity; choose an isolated lab network; no shared folders, clipboard sharing or personal credentials; name the clean snapshot baseline. Create marker.txt inside the guest, restore baseline, and record whether the marker disappeared if you actually perform the test. List excluded external disks/services. If no VM is available, label the entire restore observation unperformed and retain the completed paper design.
guide.challenge: Compare two proposed labs: A mounts your entire home directory writable into a container; B uses a clean VM with no shared folders and invented data. Explain the extra exposure in A and propose a minimal change.
guide.challenge_solution: A grants access to unrelated personal files and expands consequences of a compromised process. Remove the broad mount, share only an explicit disposable directory if needed and choose a VM boundary for workloads that require it. Neither configuration is a universal containment guarantee.

B04.concept: A virtual machine runs a guest operating system on virtual hardware. A container isolates a process environment while sharing the host kernel. A snapshot records a recoverable state under the platform's rules; it is not a substitute for a separate backup or for safe network configuration. These mechanisms provide different boundaries and failure modes.
B04.mechanism: Build labs deliberately: use synthetic data, host-only or isolated networks when required, explicit port exposure, and a known reset procedure. Sharing a host folder or mounting a privileged socket can cross the boundary you intended to create. Record the image version and configuration so that results can be reproduced rather than depending on an undocumented machine state.
B04.example: Create a harmless local lab, record its network mode, and verify which ports are reachable from the host. Save a known-good snapshot or reproducible container configuration. Change a test file and restore the baseline. Confirm what was restored and whether shared host files remained outside the snapshot's scope.
B04.pitfall: A container is not an independent kernel. Do not treat an ordinary container as sufficient isolation for unknown malware.

check.question: Which resource do ordinary containers typically share with their host?
choices: A completely independent physical CPU
The operating-system kernel
A separate guest kernel by definition
check.explanation: Containers usually share the host kernel, while virtual machines ordinarily run their own guest kernel.

guide.bridge: Builds on B04 lab boundaries, B03 API flow and O02 security goals. Use a fictional note service as the shared example.
guide.teaching:
Threat modelling asks what you are protecting, from whom, at which boundary and under which assumptions. Start with an asset and an undesirable outcome. “The app is insecure” is too vague to guide a repair; “a caller reads another account's note” is testable.

Draw actors, processes, data stores and flows. A trust boundary marks a change in assumptions, such as a browser request entering the server or a server accessing a third-party service. Identify the principal responsible for each decision. The browser may help the user choose an object, but the server must authorise the requested object independently.

For each threat, connect a control to a verification case and residual risk. A control can prevent, detect or reduce consequences without eliminating the entire threat. Prioritisation considers likelihood, impact, exposure and recovery cost. Keep assumptions visible: if your model assumes the identity provider is trusted, say so rather than presenting the conclusion as unconditional.

Use the vocabulary of the chosen model explicitly. A principal can be a user, service or delegated identity. In OS access-control discussions a subject often means an active process, although the optional lecture uses a narrower person-oriented definition. A policy states who may do what to which assets under which conditions; “need to know” alone does not specify an enforceable decision. A trusted component is one whose failure can violate that policy. Listing it in the trust boundary is an assumption to justify, not evidence that it cannot fail.
guide.example:
Asset: private note contents
Flow: browser -> API -> database
Boundary: client-controlled request enters API
Threat: caller A requests note owned by B
Control: derive caller from verified session; query by id AND owner
Check: A can read A1, cannot read B1
Residual risk: compromised A session can still read A's own notes
Assumption: session verification and database isolation work as specified
guide.explanation: The control is attached to the API decision, not merely to a hidden UI button. A negative ownership case makes the claim falsifiable. Residual risk identifies what this control cannot solve, such as a stolen session belonging to the owner.
guide.exercise: For a fictional backup download endpoint, identify asset, caller, data flow, trust boundary, one confidentiality threat, a server-side control and two verification cases. Use accounts A/B and backups A1/B1.
guide.solution: A must retrieve A1 and be denied B1. The owner should come from authenticated identity, and the lookup must constrain ownership. Hiding B1 in a list is insufficient. Record assumptions about storage access and signed download URLs.
guide.challenge: Extend the fictional note-service model with unauthorised overwrite (integrity) and exhausted storage (availability). Use impact 1=minor/reversible, 2=temporary loss of service, 3=loss of private or irreplaceable data; likelihood 1=requires unusual access, 2=plausible misuse, 3=easy through an exposed function. Multiply the two scores as a practice priority aid, justify your assumptions and choose one consequence-reducing control. This ordinal exercise is not a calibrated financial-risk model.
guide.challenge_solution: One possible ranking: unauthorised overwrite impact 3 × likelihood 2 = 6 if recovery is uncertain; storage exhaustion impact 2 × likelihood 3 = 6 if uploads are publicly available. Equal scores do not mean identical risks: explain recovery costs and uncertainty. Versioned backups can reduce overwrite consequences; per-account quotas limit one account’s storage consumption. Neither prevents every initiating event. Check each threat has an affected asset, an entry point, a control and a verification case; different justified assumptions can change the order.

S01.concept: Threat modelling starts with what the system does and what must remain true. Identify assets, actors, entry points, data flows, and trust boundaries. A threat is a possible unwanted event; a vulnerability is a weakness that can enable it; a control changes the likelihood or impact. State assumptions so another person can challenge them.
S01.mechanism: Secure design principles help turn a diagram into decisions. Least privilege limits granted authority. Complete mediation checks each relevant access. Fail-safe defaults deny access unless allowed. Defence in depth uses controls with different failure modes. Every control has costs and limits, so connect it to an actual threat rather than collecting controls without a reason.
S01.example: Draw a private notes service with browser, server, database, and backup store. Mark where identity is established and where note ownership is checked. Consider a stolen session and an accidental public backup. Add one preventive and one recovery control for each, and explain the residual risk after those controls fail or succeed.
S01.pitfall: A threat model is a revisable argument, not a guarantee. Update it when data flows, dependencies, or assumptions change.

check.question: Which is the strongest starting point for a threat model?
choices: The system's assets, behaviour, actors, and trust boundaries
A list of fashionable security tools
A promise that the framework is secure by default
check.explanation: Controls make sense in relation to what the system must protect and where untrusted influence enters.

guide.bridge: Builds on S01 threats, M04 randomness and P05 Python tests. Use a venv from P06. Teaching API: Python cryptography AESGCM; install cryptography==50.0.2 using python -m pip inside that venv. No real secrets.
guide.teaching:
Start with a note you want to keep private. Plaintext is the original bytes; ciphertext is the encrypted bytes; the key is the secret needed to recover them. A tag is a short authentication value checked during decryption. Associated data is public context such as a format label: changing it should make verification fail even though it is not encrypted. A nonce is a per-encryption input; 12 bytes × 8 bits = 96 bits. The cipher name AES-GCM identifies the specific standard construction, not a mode you need to implement yourself.

Encryption protects message confidentiality under a key. Authenticated encryption also detects unauthorised changes. AES-GCM takes a secret key, a nonce, plaintext and optional associated data. Associated data is authenticated but not encrypted, making it useful for binding a message to a public context such as a format version.

The nonce must not repeat with the same key. It is not a password and need not be secret. This small exercise generates a fresh key and a single random96-bit nonce for one encryption. Real long-lived services need a deliberate uniqueness strategy and usage limits; randomly generating values forever is not a complete key-management design.

The returned ciphertext contains an authentication tag in this API. Decryption must verify it before plaintext is used. InvalidTag can indicate changed ciphertext, wrong key, nonce or associated data; it does not uniquely identify the cause. Never replace a verification failure with unauthenticated plaintext or invent your own cipher from basic operations.

XOR (written \(\oplus\)) compares bits: equal bits give 0; different bits give 1. For the conceptual XOR example, let \(m=101\) and an independent uniform one-use pad \(k=011\). Then \(c=m\oplus k=110\), and \(c\oplus k=101\). Reusing that pad for \(m_2=001\) gives \(c_2=010\), exposing \(c\oplus c_2=m\oplus m_2=100\). Correct decryption alone therefore does not establish security. This is paper reasoning, not a cipher to implement. A keyed pseudorandom function is deterministic for a fixed key and input; its outputs are intended to look like a random function to an efficient observer who lacks the key. That is a computational assumption, unlike an ideal one-time pad’s perfect secrecy.

Nonce and IV requirements depend on the construction: uniqueness and unpredictability are different properties. For AES-GCM, preserve the same-key nonce-uniqueness rule in the API. A random generator can collide; concurrent writers, restored backups and counter wraparound need a design. Bare CTR encryption also needs every counter-block input under the same key to be distinct, including blocks inside different messages. Use the AEAD library, not a hand-built stream or an arbitrary encryption/MAC combination. A valid tag does not reject an exact replay by itself; freshness needs a protocol-level rule.
guide.example:
import os
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import AESGCM
from cryptography.exceptions import InvalidTag
key = AESGCM.generate_key(bit_length=256)
nonce = os.urandom(12)
aead = AESGCM(key)
aad = b"notes-format-v1"
ct = aead.encrypt(nonce, b"practice note", aad)
assert aead.decrypt(nonce, ct, aad) == b"practice note"
changed = bytes([ct[0] ^ 1]) + ct[1:]
try:
    aead.decrypt(nonce, changed, aad)
except InvalidTag:
    print("modified ciphertext rejected")
# Fresh key per run; never save or publish the generated key.
guide.explanation: Encryption occurs once, so the demonstration does not reuse a nonce for another encryption. The tamper test changes one bit of ciphertext and submits it for verification. Decrypting the original repeatedly is not nonce reuse for encryption. The demonstration discards its key when it ends; a service that needs later recovery must protect and persist keys separately.
guide.exercise: Run this exact harmless example in the venv. Add negative decryption tests using aad=b"notes-format-v2" and a fresh wrong key. Record round-trip success and each rejection without writing the key or ciphertext into public notes.
guide.solution:
The original decrypt assertion passes; the existing modified-ciphertext case prints its rejection. Add these tests after that example. Each tries decryption only, so no second encryption reuses the nonce.

```python
for label, candidate, context in [
    ("wrong context", aead, b"notes-format-v2"),
    ("wrong key", AESGCM(AESGCM.generate_key(bit_length=256)), aad),
]:
    try:
```
