Mass assignment happens when a server blindly applies supplied fields to its internal object. Define writable fields explicitly and derive protected fields such as owner or role from trusted state. Schema validation should reject unexpected types, unknown operations and oversized collections.

Documentation helps reviewers find intended endpoints but does not itself enforce them. Test every operation with owner, non-owner and unauthenticated identities. Include a positive case so that returning errors for every request cannot masquerade as a working authorisation system.
guide.example:
Objects: n1={owner:A,body:"one"}; n2={owner:B,body:"two"}
PATCH /notes/{id}: body field only; max100 chars
A PATCH n1 {body:"new"} -> allow
A PATCH n2 {body:"new"} -> deny ownership
A PATCH n1 {owner:"B"}  -> reject protected field
A PATCH n1 {body:7}     -> reject type
No identity PATCH n1   -> deny authentication
guide.explanation: The ownership decision uses the stored object and authenticated principal. Rejecting an owner field prevents the request from changing the very state used to authorise it. The policy can consistently reject all unknown keys rather than silently accepting misspellings.
guide.exercise: Build the five-case test matrix above and add B reading n2, B reading n1 and A updating a101-character body. Identify whether each failure is authentication, object access or schema validation.
guide.solution: A PATCH n1 with a string body is allowed. A PATCH n2 fails object access. A supplying owner fails the writable-field schema. A supplying body 7 fails type validation. No-identity PATCH fails authentication. Added cases: B reading n2 is allowed; B reading n1 fails object access; A updating n1 with 101 characters fails the 100-character limit. Check both returned response and stored object: denied cases must leave it unchanged.
guide.challenge: Add an internal audit_only field that ordinary users cannot read. Define response fields and update fields separately, then describe how you would test that a normal GET does not expose audit_only.
guide.challenge_solution: One policy returns only id and body on ordinary GET; owner may be used internally without being returned, and audit_only is never included. The PATCH writable allowlist contains only body. Given n1 with audit_only="internal-demo", test that A’s GET includes the expected body but no audit_only key, that A cannot PATCH audit_only, and that B cannot GET n1 at all. Inspect the raw JSON response as well as the visible UI; hiding a received field does not protect it.

W11.concept: An API exposes operations and data structures through documented interfaces. Object-level access control determines whether the current actor may use the object named by an ID. Guess-resistant identifiers can reduce enumeration but do not replace permission checks. An opaque ID can still be leaked, copied, or supplied by a different legitimate account.
W11.mechanism: Validate type, range, allowed fields, relationships, and requested operation. Avoid mass assignment, where arbitrary supplied fields automatically become object attributes. Separate response schemas from internal storage schemas so sensitive fields are not returned accidentally. Test the same operation with multiple controlled identities and object ownership combinations.
W11.example: Create two synthetic accounts and one private note per account. Build a test matrix for read, update, and delete using each identity and each note ID. Add an unexpected owner_id field to a local update request and ensure the server does not silently reassign ownership. Record the expected result for every row before running the tests.
W11.pitfall: API documentation describes intended behaviour; it does not enforce it. The implementation must reject forbidden combinations.

check.question: What should happen when a valid user supplies another user's private object ID?
choices: The ID's existence automatically grants access
The browser decides whether the database should return it
The server applies object-level permission checks and denies unauthorised access
check.explanation: The server must evaluate the actor-object-action relationship on every relevant operation.

guide.bridge: Builds on S06 sessions, S03 password verification and W11 validation. The recovery flow uses fictional tokens only.
guide.teaching:
A state machine is a list of allowed states and rules for moving between them. A reset token can move from issued/unused to consumed after a valid redemption, or to expired when its deadline passes. A later request must inspect its current state rather than assume the earlier unused value still holds.

Login and recovery are state machines. A recovery request should not automatically authenticate a user. A reset token needs unpredictable generation, bounded lifetime, purpose binding and one-time consumption. Store and validate it according to the selected framework rather than inventing a reversible account-id encoding.

Enumeration occurs when responses reveal whether an account exists. Similar wording alone may not remove timing or rate differences, so review the complete observable flow. Apply abuse controls without locking legitimate users out indefinitely or allowing an attacker to exhaust a shared resource.

Successful password reset should follow a deliberate session policy: rotate or revoke existing sessions as required, and notify through the intended trusted channel without including the new password. The training exercise is a paper trace, so it sends no emails and does not ask you to test real identities.
guide.example:
Fictional reset state
Token R1: account A, purpose password-reset, expires at12:00, unused
11:59 R1 + valid new password -> accept, mark used
11:59 R1 second submission     -> reject used
12:01 fresh unused R1 scenario -> reject expired
R1 used as login session      -> reject wrong purpose
guide.explanation: The second row follows the first, while the expired row is a separate fresh-state scenario. Keeping those sequences explicit prevents impossible test expectations. Token validation and consumption should be atomic enough that concurrent attempts cannot both succeed.
guide.exercise: Trace the four supplied cases. Add a token for account B submitted to reset A, and a request with no token. State what must be checked and what a generic public response should avoid disclosing.
guide.solution: Bind account/purpose, check expiry and unused state, then consume deliberately. Foreign-account and absent tokens reject. Public messages should avoid unnecessary account-existence disclosure; internal logs can retain safe reason codes.
guide.challenge: Draw reset-request, issued, consumed and expired states. Give one concurrent-use test and one verification that a reset token cannot be used as an ordinary session credential.
guide.challenge_solution: Paper transitions: request → issued/unused after approved generation; issued/unused → consumed after valid account/purpose/time checks and atomic redemption; issued/unused → expired at the deadline. Consumed and expired tokens cannot return to unused; a new request issues a different token. Concurrent case: two redemptions of the same unused token reach the protected consume step; at most one succeeds and the other sees consumed. Purpose case: submit the reset token to the ordinary session validator and expect rejection even before considering object access. Document whether a real password reset revokes old sessions; do not assume it does.

W12.concept: Authentication is a lifecycle, including registration, login, session creation, recovery, factor changes, and account closure. A strong login can be undermined by a weak recovery path. Account enumeration exposes whether an identity exists through responses, timing, or side effects, which can support later abuse depending on the threat model.
W12.mechanism: Use established framework mechanisms for credential handling, secure session rotation, recovery tokens, and appropriate rate limits. Recovery tokens need sufficient unpredictability, a limited lifetime, and carefully enforced single use. Protect factor changes as sensitive actions. Error messages should avoid unnecessary disclosure while remaining usable for legitimate users.
W12.example: Draw a test account's normal login and lost-password paths. For a local recovery flow, test an expired token, a reused token, and a token presented for the wrong account. Confirm that a successful reset changes the intended credential and follows the application's session-revocation policy. Use only synthetic accounts in the training environment.
W12.pitfall: A recovery message can be generic while other observable differences still reveal account existence. Examine the complete behaviour.

check.question: Which path deserves the same security attention as normal login?
choices: Password and multifactor recovery
Only the public colour-theme switch
Only the site's logo download
check.explanation: Recovery can confer account access, so its authority and abuse resistance are part of authentication security.

guide.bridge: Builds on W11 object/property controls and W12 identity lifecycle. Use a fictional invoice service.
guide.teaching:
Business rules constrain allowed transitions, not only reads. An invoice may be editable in draft but immutable after approval. The caller's role, object ownership and current state all matter at the moment the operation commits.

A hidden button and an unguessable identifier do not enforce a business rule. A server endpoint must check the current object under the authenticated principal. Apply the same invariant across web, API, bulk and background paths; one unprotected alternative can undermine the protected main screen.

Write a permission matrix before implementing branches. Include deny cases, but also ordinary owner actions and boundary states. For multi-step operations, use transaction/consistency mechanisms so a state change between check and update cannot authorise an invalid action.
guide.example:
Policy: owner edits draft invoice only; reviewer approves; no one edits approved totals.
I1: owner A, draft, total100
I2: owner B, approved, total200
A edit I1 -> yes
A edit I2 -> no
B edit I2 -> no (state)
Reviewer approve I1 -> yes
Reviewer edit approved I2 -> no
guide.explanation: B owns I2 but the approved-state invariant still denies editing. A reviewer role grants approval, not arbitrary alteration. These distinctions should be visible in the tests rather than encoded as “admin can do everything.”
guide.exercise: Evaluate the five supplied cases and add an unauthenticated edit, an owner edit after concurrent approval and a bulk-edit endpoint containing I1/I2. State an explicit partial-versus-atomic bulk policy.
guide.solution: The original five decisions are allow, deny, deny, allow, deny. No-identity edit is denied. If approval commits before the owner’s edit, the edit must see approved state and fail. For the bulk example choose all-or-nothing: A submits changes to I1 and I2; I2 fails owner/state checks, so neither change commits, including I1. A per-item-results policy could also be valid, but it must report each decision and preserve every item’s rules.
guide.challenge: Propose server checks and transaction boundaries for approve-and-lock. Give a test where two requests race, and explain why checking only the initial page-load state is insufficient.
guide.challenge_solution: Example paper schedule: editor reads I1 as draft; reviewer approves and locks I1; editor submits its old draft change. The server must check role, owner and current draft state at the protected update, so the edit fails after approval. Under a conditional-update design, the editor’s update includes state=draft and checks the affected-row count; approval changes draft→approved under the database’s selected transaction rules. If editing commits first, approval must deliberately approve that current version. Define version/locking policy rather than relying on the page’s old state.

W13.concept: Access control applies business rules to actions, not just URLs. Horizontal escalation crosses between peers' resources; vertical escalation gains a more privileged role. A business-logic flaw can violate a rule even when each individual request is syntactically valid and the user is authenticated.
W13.mechanism: Write invariants in plain language before testing. For example, an invitation can grant only the permissions the inviter is allowed to delegate, and a refund cannot exceed the amount paid. Enforce checks in the operation that changes state. Do not trust role names, prices, ownership fields, or workflow state supplied by the client.
W13.example: Model an invitation flow with owner, editor, and viewer roles. Define who may invite whom and which roles may be granted. Test each permitted and forbidden transition with controlled accounts. Include a viewer directly calling the invitation endpoint, rather than assuming a hidden button prevents that action.
W13.pitfall: Checking permissions only on page rendering leaves direct API requests unprotected.

check.question: Where should the rule 'a viewer cannot grant editor access' be enforced?
choices: Only by hiding the editor option in HTML
In the server operation that creates or changes the invitation
Only in a welcome email
check.explanation: The state-changing operation must enforce the rule regardless of how the request was constructed.

guide.bridge: Builds on S03 MACs, S04 signatures and S06 session policy. Use only the decoded teaching claims below; no real access token is required.
guide.teaching:
Read the teaching claims as labelled assertions: iss (issuer) says who issued the token; aud (audience) says which service it is intended for; exp (expiry) gives its time deadline. A bearer token grants usable authority to whoever holds it, so avoid copying real tokens into notes. The algorithm is the verification method; RS256 is a standard RSA-signature profile, not encryption of the readable claims. The verifier must already know which issuers, keys and algorithms it trusts. All required checks must pass together.

A JWT compact representation separates encoded header, payload and signature/MAC. Decoding is not verification. Base64url makes bytes representable as text and provides no secrecy or authenticity by itself.

A verifier must use an explicit accepted algorithm/key policy and validate relevant claims such as issuer, audience and expiry. The token's own algorithm label is input, not authority to choose an insecure verifier. Key rotation and key identifiers require a trusted lookup policy; do not fetch arbitrary key material from caller-controlled locations.

A valid token still needs object authorisation and lifecycle decisions. A token may remain cryptographically valid after a user loses a role unless the system checks current state or has a deliberate revocation/expiry design. Keep access and identity tokens' purposes separate and follow the identity provider's exact documentation.
guide.example:
Verifier policy: issuer=https://issuer.example; audience=notes-api;
algorithm=selected RS256 implementation; current time=1000
A: correct signature, iss correct, aud notes-api, exp1100 -> accept
B: same but aud other-api -> reject
C: same but exp900       -> reject
D: modified payload with old signature -> reject
E: decoded claims only, no verification -> never treat as authenticated
guide.explanation: All claim values are fictional. The fixture avoids hand-writing a verifier: a maintained JWT library must handle signature encoding and cryptographic validation. Token acceptance is a conjunction of required checks, not a choice of whichever check succeeds.
guide.exercise: Evaluate all five cases and add a correct signature with the wrong issuer and a token requesting an unsupported algorithm. State which policy check rejects each.
guide.solution: Only A is accepted. Wrong audience, expired, modified, unverified, wrong issuer and unsupported algorithm reject for their respective reasons. A valid signature does not waive claim requirements.
guide.challenge: A token for user A is valid for notes-api and unexpired. A requests B's note. Explain both token validation and the separate object decision, including a test that distinguishes them.
guide.challenge_solution: Token validation authenticates A under the policy; ownership still denies B's note. Test A's own note as allowed and B's as denied using the same valid token. Never interpret successful JWT verification as universal data access.

W14.concept: A JSON Web Token is a structured format that can carry claims. A typical signed compact token contains encoded header, payload, and signature components. Encoding makes the claims readable; it does not encrypt them. A signature can protect integrity only when the verifier uses the intended algorithm, trusted key, and appropriate claim validation.
W14.mechanism: Validate the token's issuer, audience, time constraints, algorithm policy, and purpose according to the protocol. Key selection must not become an arbitrary caller-controlled file or network lookup. A correctly signed token for a different service should not automatically work here. Consider revocation, rotation, and how long a stolen bearer token remains usable.
W14.example: Decode a synthetic course token without treating decoding as verification. List which claims are visible. Then use the provider's supported verification library to test valid, expired, wrong-audience, and altered tokens. Document the trusted key source separately from any untrusted key identifier in the token header.
W14.pitfall: A library returning decoded JSON may not have verified authenticity. Read the API contract carefully.

check.question: Does base64url-decoding a JWT establish its authenticity?
choices: Yes; readable JSON is proof of a valid signature
Yes; a token with three parts cannot be altered
No; signature and claim validation are separate required checks
check.explanation: Decoding only interprets the representation. Verification establishes integrity under a trusted key and validation policy.

guide.bridge: Builds on W14 token purposes, W04 request binding and N06 redirects. Trace the invented flow rather than connecting an actual provider.
guide.teaching:
Example: you ask a printing app to read one album from a photo service without giving it your photo-service password. You are the resource owner; the printing app is the client; the authorisation server asks for approval and issues bounded credentials; the resource server holds the photos and checks those credentials. The last two roles can belong to one company but have different jobs. A scope names permitted access. A redirect URI is the registered return address for the interaction. In a server-mediated client, a back channel is a direct client-server exchange rather than a value carried through a browser redirect; browser-only clients have a different deployment shape.

OAuth delegates access; an identity layer such as OpenID Connect adds specific authentication semantics. Distinguish resource owner, client, authorisation server and resource server. The client receives a bounded grant rather than the user's password for arbitrary reuse.

In the authorisation-code flow, the client sends the browser to an authorisation endpoint and receives a code through an approved redirect. PKCE binds code redemption to a secret verifier created by the client; state binds the browser response to the intended interaction under the client's CSRF design. Neither parameter is a substitute for validating the redirect and token purpose.

Use the provider's supported library and exact registered callbacks. A code is short-lived and not a resource access token. Validate issuer, audience and nonce as applicable to the selected identity protocol. Distinguish what the browser carries from what the client exchanges on a back channel, and avoid logging codes or tokens.

The assigned legacy implicit-flow lab has a specific additional bug: the application accepts a claimed email from the browser without binding it to verified provider identity. In the written repair, obtain identity through the intended validated identity protocol rather than trusting that field. A URL fragment after # is available to page script but is not sent in the HTTP Referer header. Prefer the authorisation-code flow under RFC 9700; public clients use PKCE and cannot safely keep a fixed client secret. A server-mediated application is one architecture, not the definition of every secure OAuth client. Issuer, audience, redirect, transaction binding and token-purpose checks remain necessary.
guide.example:
Invented trace
Client chooses state=S1 and verifier=V1; sends challenge derived from V1.
Browser -> authorisation server: client ID, exact redirect, stateS1, challenge.
Browser -> approved callback: codeC1, stateS1.
Client checks state, redeems C1 with V1 under provider rules.
Resource call uses the resulting access token for its intended audience.
Wrong returned stateS2 -> stop before treating flow as successful.
guide.explanation: The values are labels, not secure random implementations. A redirect carrying a code does not by itself prove success. The receiver must bind it to the initiating transaction and complete the protocol correctly. An access token intended for another API is not interchangeable.
guide.exercise: Draw the five steps and label browser versus client/server exchanges. Evaluate wrong state, wrong PKCE verifier and unregistered redirect scenarios. State where each should fail.
guide.solution: Step 1 happens inside the initiating client: create transaction state and a verifier. Step 2 navigates the browser to the authorisation server. Step 3 redirects that browser back to the registered client callback with code and state. Step 4 is the client’s code-redemption exchange with the token endpoint; a server-mediated client does this from its backend, while a supported browser client follows its provider’s architecture. Step 5 sends the resulting access token to the intended resource API. Wrong state fails client transaction validation; wrong verifier fails PKCE redemption at the authorisation server; an unregistered redirect fails provider redirect validation. Neither a browser redirect nor a decoded token alone proves a complete successful flow.
guide.challenge: Explain why an OAuth access token is not automatically an identity assertion for your application. Define one test for wrong audience and one for a callback replay or code reuse.
guide.challenge_solution: Use the protocol's intended authentication mechanism and validate its issuer/audience/context. Wrong-audience credentials reject; a consumed code cannot establish a fresh session through replay. Provider-specific error semantics should be tested in a designated environment.

W15.concept: OAuth delegates limited access to a resource; it is not by itself a complete login identity protocol. OpenID Connect adds an identity layer with its own tokens and validation rules. Distinguish the resource owner, client, authorisation server, and resource server, and identify which party receives each code or token.
W15.mechanism: An authorisation-code flow uses carefully registered redirect URIs and transaction binding. PKCE binds code redemption to the client instance holding a verifier, helping resist code interception. State and applicable protocol-specific checks bind a response to the initiating interaction. Use maintained libraries and current provider guidance instead of inventing a flow from isolated redirect examples.
W15.example: Draw a modern authorisation-code flow with PKCE using a synthetic account in the course lab. Label the authorisation code, verifier, access token, and any ID token. Explain why an access token for one API is not automatically a valid login assertion for a different client. Test the lab's mismatched redirect or transaction case within scope.
W15.pitfall: Access tokens and ID tokens have different audiences and purposes. Similar-looking token formats do not make them interchangeable.

check.question: What does PKCE help bind?
choices: Authorisation-code redemption to possession of the initiating client's verifier
All API permissions to the user's display name
A password to every unrelated website
check.explanation: The code challenge and verifier connect code redemption to the initiating client instance under the flow's assumptions.

guide.bridge: Builds on C07 interleavings, B02 transactions and W13 business invariants. Use the supplied paper schedule or local SQLite, not a public service.
guide.teaching:
A web race is a concurrency defect expressed through requests. If two requests both check a condition before either commits its update, each may make a decision from stale state. Sending requests quickly is a trigger, not the underlying cause.

Define the invariant first. For a one-use voucher, at most one committed redemption may exist. A robust repair makes the check and state transition atomic under the database's rules, often with a unique constraint or conditional update. A client-side disabled button does not coordinate two clients.

Retries complicate the result: a client may lose a response after a successful commit. Use a deliberately scoped idempotency key where appropriate and bind it to the same principal and operation. Returning a previously stored outcome differs from executing the state change again.

A TCP packet and an HTTP request are different units. HTTP/2 can multiplex multiple request streams over one connection; a synchronised batch can reduce network-arrival jitter, while server scheduling and database timing still vary. HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 need different synchronisation techniques. The video’s batch size is an example, not a promise of exactly simultaneous execution or a universal limit.
guide.example:
Voucher V: unused
1. Request A reads unused
2. Request B reads unused
3. A grants credit and marks used
4. B grants credit and marks used
Fault: two grants for one voucher

Repair concept: atomically claim unused V; only the successful claimant grants credit
Include claim+credit in one consistent transaction.
guide.explanation: Marking used after granting credit leaves a window. Moving the flag earlier without transaction/failure handling can instead consume the voucher without delivering credit. Both outcomes violate a complete business contract, so examine crash paths as well as concurrent success.
guide.exercise: Trace the supplied schedule and a serial order. Define the invariant and expected number of successful redemptions. Add a failure between claim and credit and state whether rollback or durable recovery is required.
guide.solution: Exactly one committed grant is permitted. Serial processing yields one success and one denial. A partial claim/credit operation needs atomic rollback or a documented durable recovery process; an in-memory flag alone is insufficient.
guide.challenge: Design request retries with keys K1 and K2 under user A. State what a repeated K1 returns, what happens when K1 is reused with a different amount and why user B cannot retrieve A's cached outcome.
guide.challenge_solution: Repeated same operation/key returns the stored outcome without another effect. Different payload under K1 rejects. Scope keys/outcomes by principal and operation, and protect their storage with the state transition. A different K2 still must obey the voucher invariant.

W16.concept: A web race condition occurs when overlapping requests violate an invariant. A limit such as 'redeem this coupon once' describes a state transition, not merely an input format. Two requests can both pass a check before either records the change. The bug lives in the interleaving of otherwise plausible operations.
W16.mechanism: Use atomic database operations, transactions with appropriate isolation, uniqueness constraints, or carefully designed locking to preserve the relevant invariant. Idempotency makes repeated equivalent requests have one intended effect, but requires a trustworthy key scope and stored result. Merely slowing requests down or adding a client-side button lock does not establish correctness.
W16.example: Model one-use redemption as unused → used. Draw two requests both observing unused, then both granting credit. Repair the local model with an atomic conditional update or an appropriate unique constraint and transaction. Test overlapping requests in the authorised lab and verify the final ledger, not just the number of successful HTTP responses.
W16.pitfall: A transaction boundary alone does not imply the isolation level needed for every invariant. State the guarantee you rely on.

check.question: What must a single-use redemption protect?
choices: Only the visual button's disabled state
The eligibility check and state change as one invariant-preserving operation
Only the time between two browser clicks
check.explanation: The server must prevent competing operations from both consuming the same entitlement.

guide.bridge: Builds on N06 HTTP framing, N04 byte streams, W01 proxy observations and C07 inconsistent state. Use paper transcripts first, then only the designated provider lab.
guide.teaching:
A proxy and backend may parse the same bytes using different rules. If they disagree where one request ends, bytes one side treats as content may be treated as a subsequent request by the other. This is a protocol-composition defect, not merely a suspicious header name.

HTTP/1.1 framing includes defined rules for message body length and transfer coding. Production fixes require strict, consistent parsing and safe handling across every hop and protocol translation. Do not create a home-made parser or rely on blocking one sample string. HTTP/2-to-HTTP/1 translation introduces its own boundary considerations.

The exercise uses a deliberately abstract parser disagreement instead of a deployable smuggling payload. Record each parser's consumed range and the remaining bytes. This makes the mechanism understandable before a provider lab introduces exact version-specific protocol rules.

For the assigned HTTP/1.1 example, Content-Length counts body octets; Transfer-Encoding: chunked introduces hexadecimal chunk lengths and chunk delimiters. CRLF consists of two bytes, carriage return (0D) and line feed (0A). A zero-sized chunk followed by the empty trailer section ends that chunked body. A parser disagreement about which bytes belong to the body can leave a prefix for the next request on a reused connection. A timeout is only a diagnostic clue; the lab checks a follow-up request too. HTTP/2 uses frames, not native HTTP/1.1 chunked transfer coding.
guide.example:
Abstract fixture: byte positions0..19
Front parser assumes body ends after position9.
Back parser assumes body ends after position14.
Bytes10..14 are therefore interpreted differently.

Parser F: request1=[0..9], next begins10
Parser B: request1=[0..14], next begins15
Question: can both sides safely reuse this connection as if aligned?
guide.explanation: Positions are inclusive: 0..9 contains 10 bytes, while 0..14 contains 15. Parser F leaves position 10 as the next request’s start; parser B treats 10..14 as part of the first request and starts the next at 15. Thus the same five bytes have conflicting meanings. The model is not valid HTTP syntax. A status code alone does not establish this parser path.
guide.exercise: Draw both boundary views for the supplied20-byte fixture. Then use matching end positions9/9 and explain the difference. State two requirements for a defensive proxy/backend configuration review.
guide.solution: Draw F as [0..9] | [10..19] and B as [0..14] | [15..19]. In the 9/9 variant both start the next request at 10, so this particular boundary disagreement is absent. That does not prove the requests or implementation are otherwise safe. Review strict framing validation, consistent interpretation through each proxy/translation hop, and how ambiguous messages are rejected and connections closed rather than reused out of alignment.
guide.challenge: Write a provider-lab evidence plan identifying scope, front/back protocol assumptions, baseline, one controlled variation, expected boundary effect and a safe stop condition. Explain why success against one parser version does not prove all deployments share the fault.
guide.challenge_solution: Parsing and translation behaviour depend on actual components/configuration. Evidence must support the tested chain and avoid extrapolation. Do not send framing experiments to unrelated production sites.

W17.concept: Request smuggling exploits disagreement between HTTP-processing components about where a request ends and the next begins. A frontend proxy and backend may interpret framing differently. The result can be a message boundary shift that affects another request. Understanding the complete proxy chain is essential before drawing conclusions from an isolated response.
W17.mechanism: Use current maintained servers and consistent protocol handling, reject ambiguous framing, and follow the deployment platform's guidance. Connection reuse and protocol translation can change exposure. This is an advanced topic because HTTP semantics, transport streams, intermediary behaviour, and isolation all interact. Keep experiments inside provider-supplied labs where no unrelated users share the connection path.
W17.example: Draw a frontend-to-backend byte stream containing two harmless requests. Mark the boundary each component expects under the lab's controlled disagreement. Explain how the two interpretations diverge without testing public infrastructure. For the remediation exercise, state which component rejects ambiguity and verify the normal request path still functions.
W17.pitfall: A timeout alone is not proof of request smuggling. It may reflect many unrelated parser or network behaviours.

check.question: What is the central failure behind request smuggling?
choices: The browser uses a long password
A database table lacks an index
Intermediaries disagree about request framing boundaries
check.explanation: Different framing interpretations let bytes acquire unintended meaning across shared connections.

guide.bridge: Builds on W01 through W17. This capstone supplies a complete fictional review packet; provider labs remain optional additional evidence.
guide.teaching:
An integrated assessment tests whether you can connect a symptom to a violated invariant and a repair that preserves ordinary use. Listing vulnerability names is weaker evidence than a reproducible authorised case with expected and actual decisions.

Use a written scope and minimise data collection. Group multiple symptoms under their root cause when they share a fix, but keep independent boundaries separate. Severity should reflect a supported failure scenario, affected data and prerequisites, not the dramatic appearance of a tool screenshot.

A remediation report includes a verification plan with both negative and positive cases. It also records what was not tested. For independent study, exchange reports with the other learner, who should be able to reproduce the reasoning from the supplied packet without access to secret data.

Separate origin, site and process. Scheme/host/effective port define an ordinary web origin; cookie eligibility follows different domain, path and request rules, and browser process allocation is an implementation detail. A classic third-party script imported by a document typically runs with that document’s authority. A cross-origin iframe is a separate document with restricted cross-origin DOM access; sandbox and messaging choices can modify the boundary. An iframe is not literally one dedicated OS process.

An HTML-text encoder protects an HTML-text insertion, not every JavaScript string, CSS expression or URL. Prefer non-executable data interfaces and textContent for plain text; use a maintained, purpose-specific sanitizer only when the product really permits rich HTML. HttpOnly can stop script from reading an eligible cookie but does not stop malicious script from issuing actions in the compromised document. A separate origin for untrusted content reduces authority only when cookies, CORS, postMessage validation, resource loading and application permissions preserve that separation. A historical browser XSS auditor is not the security boundary to rely on.
guide.example:
Fictional note API packet
A owns n1; B owns n2; body max100 chars.
Observed: A GET n2 ->200 with B's body.
Observed: PATCH n1 accepts owner=B from request body.
Observed: note preview inserts body using innerHTML despite plain-text contract.
Observed: A GET n1 ->200; B GET n2 ->200.
Scope: analyse packet only; make no external requests.
guide.explanation: The first observation is object-authorisation failure, the second protected-property assignment, and the third a text/markup boundary problem. The packet supports design findings without requiring attack execution. Existing valid owner reads are essential regression cases.
guide.exercise: Write three findings from the packet. Each needs problem, exact evidence, plausible impact, root cause, minimal repair and positive/negative verification cases. Include a scope and untested-behaviour section.
guide.solution: Scope: analyse only the supplied fictional packet; no external requests were made. Untested: runtime exploitability, other endpoints, concurrency, deployment and real data. Finding 1 — cross-owner note disclosure. Evidence: A GET n2 returned 200 with B’s body although B owns n2. The intended rule is that each learner reads only their own notes. The supported impact is disclosure of that private note; the packet does not establish access to every note. Root cause: missing or ineffective object-owner enforcement on this read path. Repair: derive A from verified identity and constrain the object lookup/authorisation by owner. Recheck A/n1 and B/n2 succeed; A/n2 and B/n1 deny without bodies. Finding 2 — protected-field assignment. Evidence: PATCH n1 accepts owner=B from caller-controlled data. This can break the ownership policy; downstream effects need separate evidence. Root cause: a writable contract that includes or blindly copies a protected field. Repair: accept only the documented body field, derive owner from trusted state and reject unknown/protected keys. Recheck an ordinary permitted body update succeeds; supplied owner, wrong types and oversized bodies reject and leave ownership unchanged. Cover single and bulk update paths. Finding 3 — unsafe plain-text preview. Evidence: the preview uses innerHTML for a body whose contract is plain text. This establishes an unintended HTML-parsing boundary; it does not alone prove executable XSS under the deployed browser/policy. Repair: render body with textContent. Recheck ordinary text still displays and practice remains literal with no nested b element. Cover main, preview and export renderers rather than only one screen. A complete report keeps observed facts separate from predicted effects and records the regression result for each path.
guide.challenge: Independently review a changed packet: ownership checks are fixed, but the export preview still uses innerHTML and bulk PATCH still accepts owner. State which original findings remain, identify the alternate paths and propose a regression matrix.
guide.challenge_solution: The object-read finding can close only for verified paths. Rendering and protected-field issues remain in alternate paths. Include main/export views and single/bulk writes. A fix in the primary screen does not establish coverage of every entrypoint.

W18.concept: An integrated assessment connects individual weaknesses to the application's security model. Begin with scope, assets, roles, data flows, and intended business rules. Build an inventory of operations and trust boundaries before selecting tests. A useful result explains the violated property, necessary conditions, reproducible evidence, and practical effect.
W18.mechanism: Separate discovery from reporting. Keep baseline requests, controlled account identities, timestamps, and minimal evidence. Confirm findings independently and avoid counting several symptoms of one root cause as unrelated successes. A repair is incomplete until it preserves legitimate behaviour and rejects the original unauthorised operation and meaningful variants.
W18.example: Assess the supplied application using an owner, a second user, and a logged-out session. Cover input handling, ownership, authentication lifecycle, cross-origin behaviour, file boundaries, and concurrent state changes. Rank findings by supported impact and likelihood. Repair at least one issue, add a regression check, and ask the other learner to reproduce the finding from the report alone.
W18.pitfall: A long tool output is not an assessment report. Explain which observed behaviour violates which rule and what evidence supports that conclusion.

check.question: What best demonstrates a finding is reproducible?
choices: Another learner can follow the scoped report and observe the same violated property
The original tester remembers the steps
The scanner lists many severity labels
check.explanation: Independent reproduction checks that the report contains sufficient evidence and instructions rather than relying on hidden knowledge.

guide.bridge: Builds on C04 pointer lifetime, C05 machine execution and C02 bounds. This exercise is a memory-layout model; do not execute invalid memory accesses.
guide.teaching:
Memory corruption violates the intended boundaries or lifetime of an object. A write beyond an array may affect adjacent data; a use-after-free accesses an object after its lifetime ends. The visible consequence depends on layout, compiler and runtime, so one crash pattern is not the definition of the defect.

Reason from source-level cause to affected invariant. If an array has capacity 4 and a routine writes 5 bytes, the bounds violation exists even if the adjacent byte happens to be unused in one build. An exploitability claim needs additional evidence about reachable input, layout and protections. Do not equate every crash with arbitrary code execution.

The repair should remove the invalid operation and preserve valid inputs. Use capacity-aware interfaces, explicit ownership and memory-safe representations where possible. Sanitizers can reveal classes of invalid access during tests, but a clean test run does not prove every path safe.
guide.example:
Abstract memory (not an actual compiler layout)
index: 0 1 2 3 | adjacent object
array: A B C 0 | flag=0
capacity4 includes terminator.
Attempt to store "ABCDE" plus terminator needs6 bytes.
Root cause: required size6 exceeds capacity4.
Repair policy: reject input; do not perform a partial unsafe write.
guide.explanation: The 0 in the array is the zero-valued terminating byte, not the printable digit "0". Five ASCII letters plus that byte need 6 slots. The model makes the arithmetic visible without relying on a platform-specific layout; the neighbouring flag is illustrative, not a promise about an actual C stack. Reject before copying. If you checked only after copying, the invalid write would already have happened.
guide.exercise: For capacity 8, calculate required bytes for ASCII strings of lengths 0,7,8 and12 with a terminator. Classify accepted/rejected inputs under a no-truncation policy. State a separate lifetime defect not captured by this capacity check.
guide.solution: Add one terminating byte: lengths 0, 7, 8 and 12 require 1, 8, 9 and 13 bytes. With capacity 8 and no truncation, accept lengths 0 and 7; reject 8 and 12 before writing. Capacity and lifetime are different: a pointer to an already freed 8-byte allocation is invalid even for a one-byte access.
guide.challenge: Write a root-cause report for a hypothetical copy of 10 bytes into an8-byte object. Separate proven bounds failure, possible consequences and evidence still needed before claiming exploitability.
guide.challenge_solution: Proven in the model: writing 10 bytes into an 8-byte object exceeds capacity by 2, violating the bounds invariant. Possible effects include corrupted adjacent data, a crash or control-flow impact, but the packet does not prove which occurs. Needed evidence includes input reachability, actual layout, first invalid access and applicable protections. Repair the size/lifetime contract and test required sizes 7, 8 and 9: first two fit this 8-byte object, the last rejects.

F01.concept: Memory corruption breaks the program's intended relationship between bytes, objects, and control flow. An out-of-bounds write may overwrite neighbouring data; use-after-free may let code access storage whose lifetime has ended. The resulting behaviour depends on layout, allocator decisions, compilation, and the surrounding program, not simply on the source line's appearance.
F01.mechanism: Reason from a minimal failing case. Identify the allocation, capacity, lifetime, write or read, and violated condition. Distinguish a crash from demonstrated control of data or execution. Use only the course's isolated binaries and benign inputs. The learning goal is to explain the defect and repair its cause, with evidence connecting input to invalid memory access.
F01.example: Take a deliberately unsafe local buffer exercise and draw its valid range. Use a diagnostic build to identify the first invalid access. Reduce the input until the smallest reproducer remains. Replace the unsafe length assumption with an explicit capacity check, then verify both the reproducer and ordinary boundary cases.
F01.pitfall: A crash is evidence of a failure, not automatically proof of a particular exploit capability or severity.

check.question: What is the strongest first step after observing a memory-related crash?
choices: Assume arbitrary code execution has been demonstrated
Disable every diagnostic to improve speed
Find and minimise the input that causes the first invalid access
check.explanation: A minimal reproducer and diagnostic evidence support a causal explanation and a targeted repair.

guide.bridge: Builds on F01 root causes, C06 page permissions and S01 layered controls.
guide.teaching:
A mitigation makes some exploitation paths harder or detects some faults; it does not necessarily eliminate the underlying bug. Address randomisation changes layout predictability. Non-executable memory restricts where instructions execute. Stack canaries detect certain stack overwrites before a protected return path. Each has a specific scope.

A bounds-safe or memory-safe design addresses a different layer by preventing invalid access under its language/runtime guarantees. Unsafe escapes, foreign-function interfaces and logic flaws still need review. Avoid treating a language name as a complete system proof.

Evaluate defences against the same threat scenario so the comparison is meaningful. State what data an attacker controls, where corruption occurs and what check runs before a harmful action. Regression tests should verify repaired behaviour as well as the presence of a build flag. A flag appearing in a configuration file is not proof it applied to the deployed binary.

Data-execution prevention/NX and W^X are related but different: NX marks a mapping non-executable, whereas W^X is a policy against simultaneous write-and-execute permissions. A JIT may transition a page from writable to executable under a controlled protocol. Neither policy repairs an out-of-bounds write. Code-reuse attacks try to redirect control through existing executable instructions rather than injecting new instructions; this is why NX alone is incomplete. Effective ASLR depends on which mappings are randomised, usable entropy and leaks; do not infer protection solely from a flag name. Build defaults change, so inspect the actual target artifact and configuration.

A mitigation may stop a particular control-flow hijack while leaving other damage possible. A crash can occur after data has leaked or a transaction has changed state; it is also a loss of availability. Memory-safe application code can still depend on unsafe native libraries, runtimes, foreign-function interfaces or deliberately unsafe blocks. Explain the boundary of the guarantee rather than promising that one language makes the whole system secure. Page permissions constrain execution and writes at page granularity; they do not check the bounds of each C object.
guide.example:
Fault: write9 bytes into an8-byte object.
Bounds check: rejects before write -> addresses root cause.
NX: may block execution from a data page -> write can still corrupt data.
ASLR: changes addresses -> does not make9 fit into8.
Canary: may detect some overwrites -> layout/path dependent.
Memory-safe container: enforces bounds under its supported operations.
guide.explanation: The key arithmetic remains wrong under all layout mitigations. Data-only corruption may matter even when injected code cannot execute. A useful report explains the remaining consequence rather than dismissing a bug because one exploit technique is harder.
guide.exercise: Create a table for all five example controls: bounds checking, NX, ASLR, canary and a memory-safe container. For each give its prevention/detection/hardening role, assumption and one remaining risk. For one selected mitigation describe how the supported lab would inspect actual build/runtime evidence, without attempting an exploit. Paper plans must be labelled unperformed.
guide.solution: Bounds check: prevents this write if every relevant path checks the true capacity before access; lifetime defects can remain. NX: hardens execution from selected pages if permissions are applied; data corruption remains. ASLR: hardens address prediction if relevant mappings are randomised and not exposed by leaks; the overflow still exists. Canary: detects selected overwrites if the protected marker is checked before return; other objects/paths can be missed. Memory-safe container: prevents unsupported out-of-bounds access under its operation guarantees; unsafe/native interfaces or logic bugs remain. Example verification plan: in the designated Linux lab inspect the target artifact’s stack-execution metadata with the provider’s documented tool and compare it with runtime page permissions. Record platform, binary and actual observations; a build flag or paper prediction alone is not runtime verification.
guide.challenge: A reviewer says “ASLR is enabled, so the overflow is fixed.” Write a precise response and propose both a source repair and a boundary regression test.
guide.challenge_solution: ASLR does not repair the out-of-bounds operation. Check required capacity before copying or use a representation that enforces bounds; test just-below, exact-fit and over-limit input while preserving ordinary successful use.

F02.concept: Memory-safety mitigations change exploit conditions. Stack canaries detect some stack corruption, non-executable pages restrict where code runs, address randomisation makes locations less predictable, and control-flow protections constrain some transfers. Each mitigation has a scope and assumptions. None should be described as making unsafe memory operations correct.
F02.mechanism: Memory-safe language features can prevent broad defect classes when used within their guarantees, but unsafe interfaces and foreign-function boundaries still need care. Apply mitigations as layers while fixing the original lifetime or bounds defect. Compare diagnostic builds with production hardening, since a sanitiser's purpose and operational costs differ from a deployment mitigation's.
F02.example: For a provided local program, identify which hardening features are enabled using the course tooling. Draw one bug's path and annotate which layer might interrupt it and which conditions bypass that layer's scope. Repair the bug and retain the mitigation. Explain the difference between preventing an invalid write and detecting one of its consequences.
F02.pitfall: A mitigation stopping one demonstration does not prove the underlying program is memory-safe.

check.question: What does a stack canary primarily do?
choices: Detect certain stack overwrites before a protected return
Prevent all heap lifetime errors
Validate every application permission
check.explanation: A canary checks a particular integrity marker. It does not provide comprehensive bounds, lifetime, or authorisation safety.

guide.bridge: Builds on S06 least privilege and C06 kernel mediation.
guide.teaching:
Authority is what a component is allowed to do, such as read one file or open a network connection. Ambient authority is access it gets automatically from its environment rather than a narrowly supplied object. A handle or descriptor is an operating-system-managed reference through which a process can use an opened resource. Giving a parser one read-only input handle is narrower than giving it access to your whole home directory.

Privilege separation divides a system so a failure in one component has limited authority. Identify which component genuinely needs each capability. A parser that handles untrusted text may not need network access, personal files or the ability to launch programs.

A sandbox constrains a process under a platform-specific policy. Capabilities can grant access to particular objects rather than broad ambient authority. The boundary must cover inherited handles, mounts, environment and communication channels; starting a process with a low-privilege name alone does not establish confinement.

Design a narrow interface between privileged and unprivileged parts. Validate requests at the privileged side and keep the protocol small. A helper that accepts arbitrary file paths or commands may recreate the authority you tried to remove. Test legitimate work and denied operations separately.

Split a privileged service by authority, not merely into multiple files. A logger may need append-only access to one log; a parser may need no filesystem authority; a broker may expose one narrowly authorised operation. Define allowed callers, object selection, input shape and failure behaviour at each message boundary. A fixed SQL template prevents syntax injection only when values are bound correctly; it still needs caller/object checks.

A descriptor integer names an entry in that process’s kernel-managed table. Guessing another integer cannot grant an unopened file, but an inherited or deliberately passed handle can carry real authority. Close unneeded handles before untrusted work. Plain chroot changes path resolution; it is not a complete sandbox and does not revoke existing descriptors or other powers. Software fault isolation similarly relies on the validator and trusted runtime enforcing exact invariants; it does not prove the isolated program is benevolent or cannot exhaust resources.
guide.example:
Design fixture: document renderer
Untrusted renderer: read one supplied input; write one output directory.
Denied: network, home directory, subprocess launch.
Privileged broker: choose input/output handles; validate size and result.
Interface: render(document_id), not run(command) or read(any_path).
Expected ordinary case: render synthetic note successfully.
guide.explanation: The broker decides which object handles the renderer receives. If it passes an unrestricted directory handle or accepts arbitrary paths, the interface may leak broader access. A successful render proves functionality, while denied-access checks provide evidence for selected confinement properties.
guide.exercise: For the renderer fixture, list assets, allowed operations and five denied operations. Define one positive test and three harmless negative tests you would perform in the supported lab. Label paper expectations separately from observed results.
guide.solution: Allowed work: read the supplied synthetic document and write its result in the designated output area. Five denials: read unrelated synthetic files; write outside the output area; make network connections; launch subprocesses; request another user’s document through the broker. Positive plan: render the supplied note and check expected output. Three harmless lab checks can attempt access to a disposable unrelated file, a forbidden loopback connection, and creation outside the output area; each should be denied under the chosen policy. These remain expectations until tested in the supported lab. A denied filesystem test does not by itself verify network or broker policy.
guide.challenge: A helper runs with broad file access and exposes copy(source,destination) to an untrusted renderer. Explain how this undermines separation and redesign the interface around explicit object authority.
guide.challenge_solution: Arbitrary source/destination paths let the renderer direct privileged operations. Replace them with validated object IDs or pre-opened constrained handles, limit output destinations and enforce caller/context rules in the broker.

F03.concept: Privilege separation divides a system into components with different authority. A sandbox constrains a component's permitted actions. A capability combines access to a resource with authority to perform specified operations. The goal is to make compromise of one part insufficient to exercise every privilege in the system.
F03.mechanism: A confused deputy is a privileged component tricked into misusing its authority for a caller. Prevent it by tying authority to the intended request and resource, avoiding ambient privileges where practical, and checking caller context. Every interface between components needs validation; moving code into a second process without narrowing its authority changes structure more than security.
F03.example: Design a document-conversion service with an untrusted parser and a separate storage component. Grant the parser access only to its input and output, not the whole archive or network. Draw the message interface and state which component authorises the requested file. Consider what an attacker could still do after taking control of the parser.
F03.pitfall: A sandbox with an unrestricted host filesystem mount can inherit the very authority it was meant to remove.

check.question: What makes privilege separation useful after one component is compromised?
choices: Every component runs as the same administrator
The compromised component has less authority than the whole service
The process names are different
check.explanation: Separating authority limits consequences. Process separation without permission separation may provide little containment.

guide.bridge: Builds on F03 containment, N02 routing and L02 permissions. Use a fictional baseline; do not change shared host firewall rules.
guide.teaching:
Hardening reduces unnecessary exposure and strengthens the components that remain. Begin with an inventory of services, accounts and required communication. Disabling a required service can cause an outage; leaving an unknown service running creates unreviewed exposure.

A baseline expresses intended state, while monitoring reports deviations. Patch policy, least privilege, backups and logging address different failure modes. Network filtering should state direction, source/destination and purpose rather than relying on an unexplained port list.

Intrusion detection evaluates evidence and can produce false positives or misses. Separate observation, rule decision and response action. Automatically isolating a host from one weak signal may cause more harm than a measured investigation. Preserve a recovery path and test rollback before applying a broad control.

Separate observation from enforcement. A passive IDS receives traffic or events and raises alerts; an IPS or other inline control may block traffic. A network sensor sees only traffic reaching its observation point and only the fields it can interpret. Encryption often hides application payloads but can leave useful connection metadata. Cloud services, remote endpoints and internal traffic may bypass a perimeter sensor, so combine network, endpoint and application evidence. VLANs divide broadcast domains; enforce the intended traffic policy with correctly placed routing, ACLs or firewalls and verify allowed and denied paths. Do not copy an older lecture’s firewall defaults or deploy TLS interception as a classroom task.
guide.example:
Fictional workstation baseline
Inbound: deny by default; no externally listening training server.
Outbound: required update/documentation services under policy.
Accounts: ordinary daily user; separate approved admin action.
Backups: versioned; weekly harmless restore check.
Logs: authentication and configuration changes with UTC/source IDs.
Alert: unexpected new listener -> investigate, not automatic proof of compromise.
guide.explanation: The baseline combines preventive and detective controls. An unexpected listener may be legitimate new software, a misconfiguration or malicious activity. Investigation should establish process identity, binding and change context before assigning intent.
guide.exercise: Create a baseline for a fictional training laptop. For each item give desired state, observation method, owner and rollback/recovery step. Analyse a synthetic alert: process demo-server listening on0.0.0.0:8765 after a local-only exercise.
guide.solution: Example rows for the fictional training laptop: (1) Training server is loopback-only; observe its documented bind address; learner owns the configuration; stop it or restore the prior loopback setting on failure. (2) Required updates remain reachable; use the platform’s normal update status rather than arbitrary scanning; device owner maintains it; roll back the scoped rule if the approved update check fails. (3) Backup can restore a disposable marker; record the actual restore result; device owner maintains copies; retain the previous known-good backup if the new check fails. For demo-server on 0.0.0.0:8765, 0.0.0.0 means all IPv4 interfaces rather than loopback only, so the bind differs from the exercise intention. Verify process identity and configuration, stop/reconfigure that training service and retest. The alert does not prove an intruder, and IPv6 exposure needs a separate check.
guide.challenge: A firewall change blocks updates and remote recovery. Explain the availability impact and write a safer rollout plan with baseline capture, one scoped change, positive/negative checks and rollback criteria.
guide.challenge_solution: Use a reversible controlled change, verify required legitimate paths and blocked unwanted paths, retain a recovery route and roll back when stated checks fail. A control is not successful merely because it blocks more traffic.

F04.concept: Hardening reduces unnecessary exposed behaviour and strengthens required behaviour. Inventory services, identities, configuration, update paths, and recovery requirements before disabling things. A firewall applies traffic policy at its position in the network path. An intrusion detector observes selected signals and alerts on patterns; it does not automatically prevent every malicious action.
F04.mechanism: Use explicit rules, least privilege, configuration baselines, and tested rollback procedures. Default-deny policies need documented allowances for legitimate traffic. Logs and monitoring should show whether controls work, while testing should verify both permitted and prohibited paths. Consider IPv6, host-local communication, and alternate interfaces instead of assuming one rule covers every route.
F04.example: For a disposable server, list listening services and define the minimum connections needed. Apply a narrow lab firewall policy, confirm the intended client still works, and verify an unwanted connection fails. Record the configuration before and after, the test source, and a recovery method in case management access is blocked.
F04.pitfall: A detector's silence is not proof that no incident occurred. It may lack the necessary visibility or rule.

check.question: What should accompany a new deny rule?
choices: Only a screenshot of the rule's name
Removal of every recovery mechanism
Tests of both the intended blocked path and required allowed paths
check.explanation: A useful control must block the threat while preserving required operation and recoverability.

guide.bridge: Builds on P06 environments, L03 version history and S01 assets.
guide.teaching:
Your app may import package A, which imports package B: B is a transitive dependency even if you never named it directly. An inventory lists those components; a software bill of materials (SBOM) is a structured form of such an inventory. An artifact is the built file or bundle you distribute. Provenance is the record of where it came from and how it was built. The dependency graph below is fictional, so this is a paper review rather than an instruction to install anything.

Software depends on packages, build tools and release infrastructure. An inventory should identify exact versions and provenance, including transitive dependencies where relevant. A familiar package name does not establish that the downloaded artifact came from the intended publisher.

Keep secrets outside committed source and public build logs. Revoking a leaked credential is different from deleting its visible line; copies and history may remain. Use short-lived, least-privilege credentials where the platform supports them, and document rotation/recovery.

Supply-chain controls can include lockfiles, verified sources, isolated builds, review and artifact provenance. None makes dependency updates unnecessary. Triage an advisory by affected version, reachability, exploit prerequisites and available fix rather than upgrading blindly or dismissing every unused-looking function without evidence.

A version contract is useful evidence, not a guarantee: a security fix can change behaviour, and the minimum acceptable version may include a particular patch. A lockfile records resolved dependencies; a reproducible build additionally requires controlled toolchains, inputs, settings and artifact verification. Vendoring transfers update responsibility to you. CI means event-triggered checks and can run on private infrastructure; passing CI does not authorise deployment or prove untested behaviour. Separate untrusted pull-request code from release credentials and review what a workflow actually executes.
guide.example:
Synthetic inventory
app -> parser-lib1.2 -> text-core3.0
Advisory: parser-lib versions below1.3 mishandle oversized records.
App accepts untrusted records through parser-lib.
Plan: reproduce with harmless fixture; update to fixed supported version;
verify normal/oversized cases; record lockfile and artifact source.
No real package names or model calls are involved.
guide.explanation: The dependency is reachable from the app's input path, so the advisory is relevant under the fixture. A version comparison alone does not prove exploitability, but the observed call path strengthens the prioritisation. Record any temporary size limit and its residual risk.
guide.exercise: Create an inventory and triage note for the supplied graph. Add a fictional leaked read/write deployment token in an old commit. State immediate containment and longer-term history/build-log actions without using a real token.
guide.solution: Inventory: application directly uses parser-lib 1.2; parser-lib uses text-core 3.0 transitively. The advisory affects parser-lib below 1.3 and this app sends untrusted records through it, so the path is relevant. Propose the supported fixed version, normal/oversize regression cases and a release record; no real advisory or runtime reproduction is supplied. For the fictional leaked deployment token: immediately revoke/rotate it at the issuer, review possible use, update authorised consumers and reduce replacement permissions. Remove exposed copies from source/history/logs through the project’s approved process, knowing earlier clones can persist. Deleting the latest line alone leaves the old token’s authority intact unless revoked.
guide.challenge: A build uses a lockfile but downloads a tool from an unpinned script URL. Explain the uncovered dependency and propose a verifiable release record covering source, tool version, inputs and output artifact.
guide.challenge_solution: The build tool is part of the supply chain even if absent from application dependency files. Pin/verify its source and version, isolate credentials and record artifact provenance with repeatable checks.

F05.concept: Secure development makes security part of design, implementation, review, release, and maintenance. A dependency is code you trust indirectly; its version, origin, build process, and update channel matter. A secret is authority-bearing material such as a credential, not an ordinary configuration value to embed in public source or browser code.
F05.mechanism: Track dependencies and provenance, review sensitive changes, use least-privileged automation, and protect release credentials. A lockfile improves repeatability but does not prove its selected package is safe. An SBOM inventories components but does not itself remediate vulnerabilities. Plan secret rotation and incident response before exposure, and separate build-time authority from runtime authority.
F05.example: Review a tiny sample project. Identify direct and transitive dependencies, the release entry point, and where credentials would enter. Replace a synthetic hardcoded credential with a documented secret-injection mechanism and a harmless example configuration. Add a checklist covering dependency updates, code review, release verification, and credential rotation.
F05.pitfall: Removing a leaked secret from the latest file does not invalidate copies in history, logs, or caches.

check.question: What is the required response to an actually exposed live credential?
choices: Revoke or rotate it through the issuing system and investigate its use
Only rename the variable
Only delete the newest source-code line
check.explanation: The authority must be invalidated. Editing one copy does not erase already exposed copies or prevent their use.

guide.bridge: Builds on C06 process identity, L02 shell concepts and S06 permissions. Windows observation is optional if unavailable; the synthetic event exercise is platform-independent.
guide.teaching:
Read the synthetic example before thinking about system logs. $events names a variable; @(...) makes an array. [pscustomobject]@{...} creates one object with named properties. The pipe | sends those objects to the next command. Where-Object keeps objects matching a condition; -eq means equal. Select-Object chooses the properties to display. Nothing in this fixture reads or changes your computer’s logs.

PowerShell processes objects through pipelines rather than only lines of text. Select properties and filter on their types. A displayed table can omit fields or truncate values, so preserve structured output when it matters to evidence.

Windows events have providers, event IDs, timestamps and fields whose meaning depends on source/configuration. An ID without provider/context is not a complete analytic definition. Process identity, integrity and privileges also influence which actions are possible. Inspect only your own lab activity and avoid exporting personal event data into shared notes.

Start with a synthetic object so the query is reproducible on paper as well as in PowerShell. Learn the distinction between filtering before collection, filtering objects and formatting output. Formatting is a final presentation step, not a replacement for retaining the underlying structured evidence.

PowerShell normally passes structured objects between cmdlets, so sort and filter properties before formatting for display. Use full names such as Get-ChildItem and Get-Process in saved scripts; an alias familiar from another shell may have different parameters or may not exist on another platform. Inspect $PSVersionTable to record your engine version. Windows PowerShell 5.1 and PowerShell 7 can differ in module support. Keep the beginner exercise read-only and avoid elevated shells or downloaded bootstrap scripts. Registry views and on-disk hive files are related but are not interchangeable copies of every live registry entry.
guide.example:
# PowerShell synthetic objects; no system logs read
$events = @(
  [pscustomobject]@{Id=1;User='A';Result='Fail'},
  [pscustomobject]@{Id=2;User='A';Result='OK'},
  [pscustomobject]@{Id=3;User='B';Result='Fail'}
)
$events | Where-Object Result -eq 'Fail' | Select-Object Id,User
# Expected records: 1/A and3/B
guide.explanation: The query filters the Result property, then projects Id and User. It does not search a rendered text table for a substring. On a non-Windows machine without PowerShell, manually apply the same predicates and label the runtime check unperformed.
guide.exercise: Run or hand-trace the supplied objects. Filter failed events for user A only, then count failures by user. Record input records and expected output separately from any optional host observations.
guide.solution:
The A-only failure is Id 1. Add these lines after the supplied $events array if PowerShell is available; otherwise trace the same conditions on paper.

```powershell
$events | Where-Object { $_.Result -eq 'Fail' -and $_.User -eq 'A' } | Select-Object Id,User
$events | Where-Object Result -eq 'Fail' | Group-Object User | Select-Object Name,Count
```

Inside the braces, $_ means the current object and -and requires both conditions. Group-Object collects matching User values; the groups are A with Count 1 and B with Count 1. These are synthetic counts, not findings about an actual endpoint.
guide.challenge: Explain what additional metadata a real event record needs for an investigation: provider/source, time/offset, host, collection provenance and field schema. Give one reason a missing event might not prove the activity never occurred.
guide.challenge_solution: Logging can be disabled, filtered, rotated or uncollected. Event meaning requires source/schema and time context. A sound answer distinguishes missing visibility from evidence of absence.

D01.concept: Windows security analysis begins with normal administration. Accounts and groups identify principals; access-control lists grant or deny operations on objects. Services run background workloads under configured identities. The registry stores structured configuration, while event logs record selected system and application activities. PowerShell exposes objects and properties, not only lines of text.
D01.mechanism: Understand the host's baseline before interpreting an event. Record the machine, account, event source, event identifier, time convention, and collection method. Elevation changes authority and should be explicit. PowerShell scripts should use narrow targets and inspect objects before mutation, particularly on a shared or important machine.
D01.example: In a disposable Windows lab, enumerate a harmless directory's ACL and inspect a known service's configured account. Generate a benign test event using the course exercise and locate it in the relevant log. Export the event with context, then explain what it directly shows and what it cannot prove about the actor's intent.
D01.pitfall: An event identifier has meaning within its provider and context. A number alone is insufficient evidence.

check.question: What is distinctive about a normal PowerShell pipeline?
choices: It can pass structured objects with properties
It can pass only raw pixels
It automatically grants administrator access
check.explanation: PowerShell commonly passes objects. This supports property-based inspection but does not remove permission requirements.

guide.bridge: Builds on D01 Windows objects, S06 identity and S04 authenticated protocols. This is a paper domain model; no directory deployment or credential collection is required.
guide.teaching:
A directory stores identities, groups, machines and policies. Domain authentication and local object authorisation are related but separate. A valid user ticket does not automatically grant access to every file share or application.

Kerberos uses tickets and shared trust relationships to authenticate principals under its protocol. A client commonly obtains a ticket-granting ticket, then a service ticket for a named service. Time, service identity and key management matter. NTLM uses a different challenge-response model; it is not simply another name for Kerberos tickets.

Reason about who trusts which authority and what identity a service actually evaluates. Group membership and delegation can expand authority, so record the intended scope and review paths. Use invented principals for diagrams. Keep these protocol tickets distinct from Windows process/thread access tokens, which describe a local execution security context.

A key-distribution centre (KDC) is the trusted authority that supplies Kerberos tickets. A realm is the administrative authentication domain whose principals it serves. A service principal name identifies the particular service the client intends to authenticate to. Kerberos introduces that trusted centre and named principals, rather than making every service receive the user’s password directly. Initial authentication obtains a ticket-granting ticket; a later request obtains a ticket for a particular service. The service validates protocol evidence, then its application must enforce permissions. Protecting the network protocol does not make a compromised client trustworthy. Domain membership, group membership and a valid ticket are not interchangeable claims. The lecture’s old protocol variant is useful for tracing assumptions; use current Microsoft documentation for AD settings, encryption types and operational policy.
guide.example:
Invented domain EXAMPLE
User A -> authentication authority -> ticket-granting ticket
A -> ticket service -> ticket for files.example
A -> file service: presents service ticket
File service -> checks A's permissions on requested folder
A belongs Readers; B belongs Editors.
Policy: Readers read; Editors read/write.
guide.explanation: The final permission check remains necessary after authentication. A Kerberos ticket is not the same object as a Windows access token attached to a process/thread. Confusing them can lead to incorrect telemetry and detection claims.
guide.exercise: Draw the exchange and evaluate A read/write and B read/write for the stated folder. Add a resource not covered by the folder policy and explain why membership alone is insufficient to infer access there.
guide.solution: A may read but not write; B may do both. Other resources need their own policy. The diagram must identify authority, client and service rather than treating every message as a password exchange.
guide.challenge: Compare a Kerberos service ticket, an NTLM challenge-response exchange and a Windows process access token at the level of purpose and observation source. State one assumption you would verify before interpreting a log as successful service access.
guide.challenge_solution: Tickets support protocol authentication; NTLM is a distinct authentication mechanism; access tokens describe local security context. Authentication success need not mean a particular object operation succeeded. Correlate service/object authorisation evidence and source-specific event meanings.

D02.concept: Active Directory centralises identities and policy in a Windows domain. Domain controllers perform critical directory and authentication functions. Kerberos uses tickets and trusted key relationships to authenticate access to services. NTLM is a different authentication family with different properties and risks; do not treat the two as interchangeable labels.
